Question 1

When we use a hash table data structure, our hash function should map the expected inputs (keys) as evenly as possible over its output range(indexes). This property of good hash function is known as______.

  • A. Uniformity
  • B. Determinism
  • C. Continuity
  • D. Data normalization

Source

  • MOE Computer Science Exit Exam · 2016 · Question 12

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Trace the initial state and each executed operation in order, preserving the requested output layout.

Study-guide sections

DSA25 · Hash addresses, uniformity and random function choice

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA25 · Hash addresses, uniformity and random function choice

Correct answer: A — Uniformity

DSA25 defines uniformity as spreading expected keys evenly among addresses. That directly matches the question’s wording. Determinism is a different obligation: repeated equal keys receive the same address for the chosen function. Continuity and data normalization do not name this distribution property, so only Uniformity answers the literal stem.

Evidence in the complete study note

Determinism means repeated equal keys get the same address for the chosen function. Uniformity means expected keys spread evenly. Universal hashing chooses one function randomly from a suitable family for the table, independently of a fixed key set; it does not choose a fresh unrelated function for each lookup. Random choice controls collision probability, not a promise of zero collisions.DSA25

Choice by choice

A · correct — Uniformity describes spreading expected input keys evenly across the output address range, exactly as the stem requires.

B · incorrect — Determinism requires repeated equal keys to map identically; it does not require an even address distribution.

C · incorrect — Continuity is not the key-distribution property defined for hash functions in DSA25.

D · incorrect — Data normalization does not name the even-distribution requirement of a hash function.

Question 2

In a one-based array representation of a binary heap, the root is at index 1. If a node at index i has a right child, at which index is that child stored?

  • A. 2*i+1
  • B. i/2
  • C. (i+1)/2
  • D. 2*i

Adapted from

  • MOE Computer Science Exit Exam · 2016 · Question 13

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Compare the required access order and representation constraints with the defining operations of each option.

Study-guide sections

DSA23 · A heap combines completeness with a weaker ordering

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA23 · A heap combines completeness with a weaker ordering

Correct answer: A — A. 2*i+1

Heap child formulas depend on whether indexing begins at zero or one. With the explicitly stated one-based convention, the two children of node i occupy positions 2i and 2i+1. The latter is the right child. Integer division by two instead identifies a parent in this convention. The existence condition matters because an index computed beyond the current heap size does not designate an actual child.

Evidence in the complete study note

Zero-based array representation: root index 0, left=2i+1, right=2i+2, parent=floor((i-1)/2) for i>0. One-based representation uses children 2i,2i+1 and parent floor(i/2). A child exists only if its index is inside the current heap size.DSA23

Choice by choice

A · correct — 2i+1 is the one-based right-child index.

B · incorrect — floor(i/2) computes the parent for nonroot nodes.

C · incorrect — (i+1)/2 does not compute the right child.

D · incorrect — 2i is the one-based left child.

Question 3

Use iterative sequential search and iterative binary search on random-access arrays, with constant-size indices. For binary search, reverse comparisons on descending arrays. Compare tight asymptotic auxiliary space and worst-case element probes as n grows. Which statement is false?

  • A. Binary searching algorithm can work on list of data which is stored in descending order
  • B. Sequential and binary searching algorithm are not equal in terms of memory efficiency
  • C. Sequential searching algorithm can work on sorted and unsorted list of data
  • D. Binary search has a smaller tight worst-case probe order than sequential search on sorted random-access arrays.

Adapted from

  • MOE Computer Science Exit Exam · 2016 · Question 14

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Fix the input case and cost model, then count dominant work or simultaneously live storage.

Study-guide sections

DSA28 · Linear search: a scan with an early stop

DSA29 · Binary search: maintain a shrinking ordered interval

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA28 · Linear search: a scan with an early stop

DSA29 · Binary search: maintain a shrinking ordered interval

Correct answer: B — B. Sequential and binary searching algorithm are not equal in terms of memory efficiency

Both iterative algorithms keep only a fixed number of indices and temporary values, giving constant auxiliary space. Their worst-case probe counts differ: sequential search can inspect every element, whereas binary search halves the ordered interval each time. Binary search can also handle descending order with reversed comparisons, and sequential search does not require sorted input. Under these specified implementations, the unequal-memory claim is the false statement.

Evidence in the complete study note

Compare the target with successive elements until equal or exhausted. Unsorted data is allowed; sorted data is allowed too. A first-element match costs Theta(1). An absent target or last-position match needs n comparisons, giving Theta(n) worst time. Uniformly likely successful positions average (n+1)/2 comparisons, still linear.DSA28
Worst probes are floor(log₂n)+1 for n>0: seven for 100 keys, about twenty for one million. Iteration uses constant space; recursion uses logarithmic stack depth. Linked midpoint traversal loses logarithmic total time. Boundary variants retain a candidate rather than stopping at equality.DSA29

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Descending binary search works with reversed comparisons.

B · correct — Both iterative implementations use constant auxiliary space, so this inequality claim is false.

C · incorrect — A sequential scan works with either input ordering.

D · incorrect — Binary search has logarithmic rather than linear worst-case probes.

Study-guide sections

DSA37 · Merge sort and internal versus external sorting

DSA34 · Insertion sort: extend a sorted prefix

DSA33 · Selection sort: minimize exchanges, not comparisons

DSA36 · Quicksort: separate partition guarantees from exact traces

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA37 · Merge sort and internal versus external sorting

DSA34 · Insertion sort: extend a sorted prefix

DSA33 · Selection sort: minimize exchanges, not comparisons

DSA36 · Quicksort: separate partition guarantees from exact traces

Correct answer: C — C. Merge sort

Ordinary array mergesort merges two sorted halves through a temporary buffer that can hold a number of elements proportional to n. Insertion sort retains one item while shifting, and selection sort needs fixed temporary storage for a minimum position and an exchange. Ordinary quicksort partitions inside the original array. Its recursive stack is counted separately here, so the linear element-buffer requirement uniquely identifies mergesort.

Evidence in the complete study note

Ordinary array merging needs a linear auxiliary buffer.DSA37
For each remaining item, save its value, shift larger preceding values right, and insert it into the gap.DSA34
At position i, scan the remaining suffix for its minimum, then exchange it with A[i].DSA33
Quicksort normally rearranges in the same array but recursive storage can be linear in the worst case.DSA36

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Insertion saves one item and shifts within the same array.

B · incorrect — Selection retains a minimum position and a fixed-size swap temporary.

C · correct — Ordinary array merging needs a linear auxiliary element buffer.

D · incorrect — In-array partitioning needs no full merge buffer; recursive frames are excluded by the stated convention.

DSA14 · Queues preserve arrival order

DSA11 · Implement a stack with one consistent top convention

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA14 · Queues preserve arrival order

DSA11 · Implement a stack with one consistent top convention

Correct answer: D — Queue

The module explicitly identifies print-server jobs as a queue application. FIFO preserves arrival order among pending jobs. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 8, 6, 9.

Evidence in the complete study note

FIFO suits equal-priority printer jobs, shared-resource waiting, asynchronous buffers and level-order exploration. A play sequence can also use a queue. Distinguish airline seat records from waiting requests; an application name alone does not force one representation.DSA14
Stack policy is LIFO, equivalently FILO. Push inserts, pop removes/returns top, and peek only observes. With zero-based occupied slots, top=-1 is empty and top=C-1 is full. Check before A[++top]=x or returning A[top--].DSA11

D · correct — The print server maintains a queue of print jobs. See assigned PDF 8, 6, 9.

Question 6

Which one of the following is true about Queue data structure?

  • A. Queue data structure applies first come first served policy
  • B. Queue data structure uses last in first out rule
  • C. Queue data structure does not have efficient basic operations
  • D. Queue data structure cannot be implemented using linked list

Source

  • MOE Computer Science Exit Exam · 2016 · Question 76

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Compare the required access order and representation constraints with the defining operations of each option.

Study-guide sections

DSA14 · Queues preserve arrival order

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA14 · Queues preserve arrival order

Correct answer: A — Queue data structure applies first come first served policy

FIFO serves the first arrival first; the module also explicitly gives linked-list enqueue and dequeue. Therefore A is true and the supplied D key contradicts page 8. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 7, 8.

Evidence in the complete study note

An ordinary queue enqueues at rear, dequeues at front, and peeks at front. This is FIFO or first-come, first-served. A linked implementation with head and tail supports both operations in constant time: append at tail, remove at head. The first insertion sets both pointers; removing the last item clears both. With head alone, insertion must traverse to the tail.DSA14

Choice by choice

A · correct — First come first served is stated under queue applications. See assigned PDF 7, 8, 8.

B · incorrect — LIFO describes the stack, whereas queue deletion is at the front. See assigned PDF 7, 8, 8.

C · incorrect — A blanket inefficiency claim is unsupported; front removal and rear insertion can use fixed pointer updates. See assigned PDF 7, 8, 8.

D · incorrect — The module expressly implements the queue as a linked list. See assigned PDF 7, 8, 8.

An unsorted singly linked list maintains only its head pointer. Which option gives the complete set of listed operations with tight worst-case constant time? There is no cached tail, predecessor index or positional index.

  • A. Insertion at the front of the linked list
  • B. Insertion at the end of the linked list
  • C. Deletion of the front node of the linked list
  • D. Deletion of the last node of the linked list
  • E. A&C

Adapted from

  • Addis Ababa University mock exam · Question 50

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Fix the input case and cost model, then count dominant work or simultaneously live storage.

Study-guide sections

DSA09 · Update links without losing the rest of the list

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA09 · Update links without losing the rest of the list

Correct answer: E — E. A&C

Inserting at the head links the new node to the old head and updates head. Deleting the head advances head and releases one node. Both use constant work. Appending requires traversal to find the tail, and deleting the tail requires its predecessor, also found by traversal. The complete constant-time set is therefore insertion at the front together with deletion of the front, which is option E.

Evidence in the complete study note

Prepend with new.next=head; head=new. To insert after a known predecessor p, set new.next=p.next before p.next=new. Appending with only head requires a tail traversal; maintaining tail avoids it. Delete the head by saving old=head, advancing head=head.next and releasing old in C++.DSA09
Deleting the tail of a singly linked list requires its predecessor, even when tail itself is known. Handle empty and single-node lists separately; after removing the only node, set both head and tail to null. To remove a known successor, bypass it before deallocation. Clearing an owned n-node chain visits and releases every node.DSA09

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Front insertion is constant, but this alone omits the also-constant front deletion.

B · incorrect — Head-only append traverses the list to find its tail.

C · incorrect — Front deletion is constant, but this alone omits the also-constant front insertion.

D · incorrect — Tail deletion must locate its predecessor by traversal.

E · correct — This combines exactly the two listed constant-time operations.

A capacity-six circular queue uses all six slots with front=0 and size=6. Its physical array is [11,13,15,17,19,21]. After dequeue() and enqueue(9), what is the logical front-to-rear sequence?

  • A. 9, 11, 13, 15, 17, 19
  • B. 13, 15, 17, 19, 21, 9
  • C. 11, 13, 15, 17, 19, 9
  • D. Queue overflow

Study-guide sections

DSA15 · Circular buffers: logical order differs from physical slots

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA15 · Circular buffers: logical order differs from physical slots

Correct answer: B — B. 13, 15, 17, 19, 21, 9

The initial front element is 11, so dequeue removes it and advances front to the slot containing 13. The queue now has five items. Circular insertion reuses the freed physical slot zero for 9 and restores size six. Reading from the new front around to the rear gives 13,15,17,19,21,9. Physical slot order differs from this requested logical service order.

Evidence in the complete study note

A simple noncircular array queue may report overflow when rear reaches the final index despite released slots at the front. A circular queue reuses slots with modulo arithmetic. Use a count convention: front points to the next removal, size counts items, and insertion slot is (front+size)%C. Empty means size==0; full means size==C.DSA15

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — This would remove 21 and prepend 9 rather than remove the front.

B · correct — This is the front-to-rear order after removing 11 and appending 9.

C · incorrect — This incorrectly retains 11 and removes the rear 21.

D · incorrect — Circular reuse makes room for the insertion after the removal.

Question 12

A circular queue has capacity six, front=0 and size=6, using physical slots [11,13,15,17,19,21]. It can use all six slots. After dequeue() and enqueue(9), list the physical array in index order 0 through 5.

  • A. 9, 11, 13, 15, 17, 19
  • B. 13, 15, 17, 19, 21, 9
  • C. 11, 13, 15, 17, 19, 9
  • D. 9, 13, 15, 17, 19, 21

Adapted from

  • Addis Ababa University mock exam · Question 56

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Trace the initial state and each executed operation in order, preserving the requested output layout.

Study-guide sections

DSA15 · Circular buffers: logical order differs from physical slots

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA15 · Circular buffers: logical order differs from physical slots

Correct answer: D — D. 9, 13, 15, 17, 19, 21

Dequeue reads 11 at index zero, advances front to index one and reduces size to five. The count-based insertion formula then gives (front+size)%6=(1+5)%6=0. Enqueue therefore writes 9 into the freed slot zero. All other physical slots retain their old values. The logical service order begins at 13, but the requested physical index order begins at the newly stored 9.

Evidence in the complete study note

A simple noncircular array queue may report overflow when rear reaches the final index despite released slots at the front. A circular queue reuses slots with modulo arithmetic. Use a count convention: front points to the next removal, size counts items, and insertion slot is (front+size)%C. Empty means size==0; full means size==C.DSA15
Dequeue reads A[front], sets front=(front+1)%C and decreases size. An alternative reserves one unused slot and uses next(rear)==front for full; its empty test and capacity differ. State the convention before tracing.DSA15

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — This drops 21 and retains the removed 11.

B · incorrect — This is logical front-to-rear order, not physical index order.

C · incorrect — This overwrites 21 instead of reusing slot zero.

D · correct — Slot zero receives 9 and slots 1–5 remain unchanged.

  • A. Stack

Study-guide sections

DSA41 · BFS: discover one distance layer at a time

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA41 · BFS: discover one distance layer at a time

Correct answer: D — Queue

Breadth-first search repeatedly dequeues a vertex and enqueues its undiscovered neighbors. FIFO ordering ensures earlier distance layers are processed before later ones. Arrays or linked nodes can store this frontier, but Queue names its required access discipline. A stack instead serves latest pending work.

Evidence in the complete study note

Mark the source when enqueuing it. Repeatedly dequeue a vertex, examine its neighbours, and enqueue each unvisited neighbour while marking it. Store predecessor[v] when discovering v if a path must be reconstructed. FIFO ensures vertices at distance d are explored before later distance layers.DSA41

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — A stack serves the latest pending vertex first and does not preserve BFS distance-layer order.

B · incorrect — An array can store a queue, but an array alone specifies no FIFO frontier discipline.

C · incorrect — Linked nodes can represent a queue, but Linked List alone does not specify breadth-first processing.

D · correct — A FIFO queue processes discovered vertices by distance layer, the standard BFS frontier rule.

Suppose we define a static method totalEvenLoc() that returns the total for even-index items of an integer list as shown, on the right, below. What is the Big O running time of the method if lst is a LinkedList of size N? public static int totalEvenLoc(List<Integer> lst) { int sum = 0; for(int i = 0; i < lst.size(); i += 2) sum += lst.get(i); return sum; }

  • A. O(N)
  • B. O(1)
  • C. O(N^2)
  • D. O(logN)
  • E. O(NlogN)

Source

  • Mock exam 4 · Question 16

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Study-guide sections

DSA07 · Count loops and account for hidden access costs

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA07 · Count loops and account for hidden access costs

Correct answer: C — O(N²), tightly Θ(N²)

The loop visits about N/2 even indices, but LinkedList.get(i) walks from the nearer endpoint. A linear number of those indices lie near the middle, each requiring linear traversal. DSA07 analyzes exactly this access pattern and obtains Θ(N²) total work. Incrementing by two changes a constant factor, not the quadratic order.

Evidence in the complete study note

Indexed access is not constant for every List implementation. Java LinkedList.get(i) walks from the nearer endpoint. Summing get(0), get(2), get(4), … over a length-N list still gives Theta(N²), because a linear number of middle indices each require linear traversal. An iterator scans once in linear time. An exact executable runtime requires valid code and an explicit cost convention.DSA07

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — O(N) would require constant-cost indexed access; LinkedList.get(i) instead traverses nodes.

B · incorrect — A growing number of accesses and additions prevents a constant bound on total work.

C · correct — A linear number of middle-index accesses each traverse a linear number of nodes, yielding quadratic time.

D · incorrect — Neither the iteration count nor the accumulated linked-node traversal has logarithmic growth.

E · incorrect — Quadratic traversal grows faster than N log N, so this is not a valid upper bound.

Study-guide sections

DSA24 · Restore a heap after insertion or removal

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA24 · Restore a heap after insertion or removal

Correct answer: A — 6 5 4 2 1

Remove 10 by moving 5 to root and adjusting: [8,5,6,2,1,4]. Remove 8 by moving 4 to root and adjusting through child 6: [6,5,4,2,1]. These are standard root-last swaps and downward heap restoration. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 11.

Evidence in the complete study note

Insert at the next complete-tree position and swap upward while parent order is violated. To remove the root, move the final element to root, reduce heap size, then swap downward with the more dominant child until order holds. Each path has logarithmic length. Building bottom-up by sinking internal nodes takes linear total time; repeated independent insertions give an O(n log n) construction bound.DSA24
Max-heap [10,8,6,2,1,4,5]: remove 10, move 5 to root and sink, giving [8,5,6,2,1,4]. Remove 8, move 4 up then exchange with 6: [6,5,4,2,1].DSA24

Choice by choice

A · correct — Matches both root deletions and adjustment steps. See assigned PDF 11.

B · incorrect — A valid max heap, but not the result of these root-last adjustments. See assigned PDF 11.

C · incorrect — Changes the lower pair 2,1 as well as giving a different adjustment history. See assigned PDF 11.

D · incorrect — Reverses the unchanged lower pair 2,1. See assigned PDF 11.

DSA14 · Queues preserve arrival order

Study-guide references

DSA14 · Queues preserve arrival order

Correct answer: D — Both may change.

Insertion into an empty linked queue makes the new node both front and rear. Insertion into a nonempty queue changes rear while front remains. Consequently both references may change across the allowed cases. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 7, 8, 5.

An ordinary queue enqueues at rear, dequeues at front, and peeks at front. This is FIFO or first-come, first-served. Question 17

Binary search is to operate on an already ordered sequence of comparable keys through an indexed-access interface. Which listed property is required of its search domain, rather than being a particular physical array representation or allocation policy?

  • A. The array must hold elements of the same data type.
  • B. All are additional requirements.
  • C. The array must be contiguous.
  • D. The search interval must have valid finite bounds.
  • E. The array must fix its size a prior to population.
  • F. None is an additional requirement.

Adapted from

  • Mock exam 4 · Question 19

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Compare the required access order and representation constraints with the defining operations of each option.

Study-guide sections

DSA29 · Binary search: maintain a shrinking ordered interval

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA29 · Binary search: maintain a shrinking ordered interval

Correct answer: D — D. The search interval must have valid finite bounds.

Binary search maintains an interval of candidate indices and repeatedly shrinks it until a match or an empty interval is obtained. That operation requires valid finite bounds. Homogeneous physical storage and contiguity are properties of ordinary array representations, rather than requirements of the abstract interval-halving procedure. Fixing capacity before population is unnecessary: a resizable sequence can be populated first and searched afterward. Hence not all listed properties are requirements.

Evidence in the complete study note

On an ascending random-access sequence, set lo=0, hi=n-1. Compute mid=lo+(hi-lo)//2. Equality finishes; if target<A[mid], set hi=mid-1; otherwise set lo=mid+1. Stop unsuccessfully when lo>hi. Reverse comparisons for descending order. Comparable keys and valid finite bounds matter; fixed allocation before population is not an extra algorithmic requirement.DSA29

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Comparable keys are assumed; identical physical data types are not the abstract domain requirement.

B · incorrect — All fails because prior fixed allocation is unnecessary.

C · incorrect — Contiguity is a representation choice rather than the abstract search-domain requirement.

D · correct — The candidate index domain needs valid finite bounds.

E · incorrect — A resizable sequence may be populated before searching.

F · incorrect — Valid finite bounds are a required condition among these choices.

Question 18

What will be the content of the queue (shown from queue front on the left to queue rear on the right), after the given sequence of operations shown below? Queue q = new Queue(); q.enqueue(4); q.enqueue(8); if(q.peek() > 5) q.dequeue(); q.enqueue(1); q.enqueue(6); q.dequeue();

  • A. 4, 6
  • B. 4, 8, 1
  • C. 8, 1, 6
  • D. 8, 6
  • E. 4, 1

Source

Study-guide sections

DSA14 · Queues preserve arrival order

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA14 · Queues preserve arrival order

Correct answer: C — 8, 1, 6

After enqueues the queue is [4,8]. Peek examines the front 4, so 4>5 is false and the conditional dequeue does not execute. Enqueues give [4,8,1,6]; the final dequeue removes 4, leaving [8,1,6]. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 7, 6.

Evidence in the complete study note

An ordinary queue enqueues at rear, dequeues at front, and peeks at front. This is FIFO or first-come, first-served. A linked implementation with head and tail supports both operations in constant time: append at tail, remove at head. The first insertion sets both pointers; removing the last item clears both. With head alone, insertion must traverse to the tail.DSA14

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Drops 8 and 1 without corresponding deletions. See assigned PDF 7, 6.

B · incorrect — Leaves the removed 4 and omits the enqueued 6. See assigned PDF 7, 6.

C · correct — Matches the final FIFO sequence. See assigned PDF 7, 6.

D · incorrect — Incorrectly removes 1 as well as 4. See assigned PDF 7, 6.

E · incorrect — Drops 8 and 6 and retains the removed 4. See assigned PDF 7, 6.

DSA19 · BST search follows a global ordering invariant

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA19 · BST search follows a global ordering invariant

Correct answer: B — B. O(n³)

This asks about constructing an optimal BST, rather than searching a tree after construction. The standard dynamic program considers quadratically many key intervals. For each interval it tries up to a linear number of candidate roots, combining the relevant subproblem costs. Multiplying those counts gives cubic construction time. The cubic option states that bound; the linear, logarithmic and factorial alternatives do not give the tight construction order.

Evidence in the complete study note

Standard optimal-BST dynamic programming tries each possible root for each key interval: O(n²) intervals times O(n) roots gives O(n³) construction.DSA19

DSA02 · Arrays: indexed access, capacity and shifting

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA02 · Arrays: indexed access, capacity and shifting

Correct answer: A — The amount of memory to be allocated should be known beforehand.

The module calls array storage static and contrasts it with dynamically allocated nodes. A fixed array requires a capacity in advance; constant access and reuse as a storage implementation are benefits, while contiguous storage alone is not the capacity drawback. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 6, 7, 5.

Evidence in the complete study note

A fixed array has a chosen capacity; the choice need not occur at compile time. A resizable array allocates a larger block and copies when needed. Inserting in the middle shifts later elements, so it costs linear time. Appending into spare capacity is constant; a resizing append can be linear, though repeated geometric growth gives amortized constant append cost.DSA02

Question 23

For selection sort on n elements, n>=2, count only exchanges between distinct positions and omit the final one-element suffix. What is the maximum number of swaps?

  • A. n - 1
  • B. 1
  • C. n
  • D. n - 2

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Study-guide sections

DSA33 · Selection sort: minimize exchanges, not comparisons

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA33 · Selection sort: minimize exchanges, not comparisons

Correct answer: A — A. n - 1

Selection sort places the minimum remaining element into each successive position. After n-1 such placements, the last position is determined automatically. Each placement needs at most one exchange between distinct positions, so the maximum is n-1. This count excludes self-swaps and the redundant final-position call that some implementations include. The choice of input can require an exchange on every one of those meaningful passes.

Evidence in the complete study note

At position i, scan the remaining suffix for its minimum, then exchange it with A[i]. There are n-1 meaningful placements and n(n-1)/2 comparisons regardless of initial order. At most n-1 exchanges of distinct positions are needed. A loop that also swaps the last item with itself can count n swap calls.DSA33

Choice by choice

A · correct — There are n-1 meaningful placements, each requiring at most one exchange.

B · incorrect — More than one exchange can be needed for larger n.

C · incorrect — n counts an extra redundant final swap call under another convention.

D · incorrect — n-2 omits a possible exchange on a meaningful pass.

Question 24

In an infix-to-prefix conversion algorithm that temporarily holds pending operators and parentheses using last-in, first-out access, which abstract data type supplies that access discipline?

  • A. Stack
  • B. Queue
  • C. Binary tree
  • D. Linked list

Study-guide sections

DSA11 · Implement a stack with one consistent top convention

DSA13 · Infix, postfix and prefix expressions

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA11 · Implement a stack with one consistent top convention

DSA13 · Infix, postfix and prefix expressions

Correct answer: A — A. Stack

Pending operators must be retrieved in reverse order when grouping or precedence requires them to be emitted. A stack provides that last-in, first-out discipline. An expression tree is another possible representation for conversion, but it is not the requested pending-operator ADT in this specified algorithm. A queue retrieves the oldest entry first, while a linked list alone describes storage links without prescribing the needed access policy.

Evidence in the complete study note

Stack policy is LIFO, equivalently FILO. Push inserts, pop removes/returns top, and peek only observes. With zero-based occupied slots, top=-1 is empty and top=C-1 is full. Check before A[++top]=x or returning A[top--].DSA11
To evaluate postfix, push operands. At a binary operator, pop right operand first, then left, and push left op right. Build an expression tree for either prefix (preorder) or postfix (postorder); a stack is useful but is not the only possible conversion representation.DSA13

Choice by choice

A · correct — A stack retrieves the latest pending operator first.

B · incorrect — A queue uses first-in, first-out access.

C · incorrect — An expression tree can support another conversion method but is not this pending-operator ADT.

D · incorrect — A linked list can implement storage but alone does not specify LIFO behavior.

Question 28

Which listed characteristic is a binary-tree shape condition rather than a general functional-correctness or resource-cost criterion for arbitrary data-structure operations? Interpret completeness as the complete-tree shape property.

  • A. Completeness
  • B. Correctness
  • C. Time Complexity
  • D. Space Complexity

Adapted from

  • Data Structures & Algorithms practice questions · Question 5

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Compare the required access order and representation constraints with the defining operations of each option.

Study-guide sections

DSA18 · Tree vocabulary and the different binary shapes

DSA04 · Algorithm properties are separate obligations

DSA05 · Measure costs before naming their growth

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA18 · Tree vocabulary and the different binary shapes

DSA04 · Algorithm properties are separate obligations

DSA05 · Measure costs before naming their growth

Correct answer: A — A. Completeness

Correctness asks whether operations produce their specified results. Time and space complexity measure operation counts and memory use under a resource model. Completeness, under the explicit meaning supplied here, instead describes how a binary tree’s levels are filled: earlier levels are full and the last fills from the left. It is a particular shape condition, rather than a universal assessment criterion for every data structure.

Evidence in the complete study note

Binary means at most two children. Full means each node has zero or two children. Complete means all earlier levels are filled and the last fills from left. Perfect means all leaves share a level and every internal node has two children. Balanced means height stays logarithmic under a stated rule; it does not require a perfect shape.DSA18
Finiteness means termination after finitely many steps for every valid input. Definiteness means each instruction has one interpretation; effectiveness means each step is executable. Correctness means meeting the stated result for every valid input. A finite program can still return the wrong answer.DSA04
Time counts chosen operations; space counts memory, including live recursive frames.DSA05

Choice by choice

A · correct — Completeness describes a particular binary-tree shape.

B · incorrect — Correctness assesses whether an operation meets its specification.

C · incorrect — Time complexity assesses operation cost.

D · incorrect — Space complexity assesses memory cost.

DSA14 · Queues preserve arrival order

Study-guide references

DSA14 · Queues preserve arrival order

DSA16 · Deques, merging and splitting queues

Correct answers (select all): B, C — B. Queues; C. Deques

An ordinary queue supplies exactly the stated FIFO operations: insertion at the rear and removal at the front. A deque allows insertion and removal at both ends, which includes those same two operations as a subset. The question explicitly includes types with additional endpoint capabilities, so both qualify. A stack exposes a single LIFO top, and a BST organizes access by keys rather than front and rear.

Evidence in the complete study note

An ordinary queue enqueues at rear, dequeues at front, and peeks at front. This is FIFO or first-come, first-served. A linked implementation with head and tail supports both operations in constant time: append at tail, remove at head. The first insertion sets both pointers; removing the last item clears both. With head alone, insertion must traverse to the tail.DSA14
A deque permits both-end insertion/removal without guaranteeing middle access. Endpoint-linked operations are constant but middle indexing is linear. A circular-array deque may support indexed access. Dequeue names removal; deque names the structure.DSA16

Study-guide sections

DSA34 · Insertion sort: extend a sorted prefix

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA34 · Insertion sort: extend a sorted prefix

DSA36 · Quicksort: separate partition guarantees from exact traces

DSA37 · Merge sort and internal versus external sorting

DSA39 · Radix sorting uses key digits, not arbitrary magic

Correct answers (select all): B, C — B. Insertion sort; C. Quick sort

Insertion sort on reverse input shifts a growing sorted prefix, totaling quadratic work. Quicksort repeatedly choosing an extreme pivot also accumulates quadratic partition work. Ordinary merge sort instead performs linear work at logarithmically many levels. Under the explicitly fixed digit count and radix, radix sorting is linear in n. Tight bounds distinguish these actual growth rates from the looser quadratic upper bounds that faster algorithms also satisfy.

Evidence in the complete study note

Reverse order causes 1+2+…+(n-1) shifts: quadratic time.DSA34
Balanced partitions give n log n work; repeated extreme pivots sum n+(n-1)+… to quadratic work.DSA36
There are logarithmically many levels with linear merge work per level, giving n log n time even on sorted input unless an optimization skips merges.DSA37
With d digits and radix r, counting-based passes take O(d(n+r)) time and O(n+r) auxiliary storage.DSA39

Correct answers (select all): A, B, D — A. Bubble sort; B. Selection sort; D. Insertion sort

Bubble sort reuses one temporary element for each adjacent swap. Selection sort retains the minimum position while scanning, then exchanges elements using the same fixed-size temporary storage. Insertion sort saves one item and shifts preceding entries within the original array before filling the gap. The indices and saved elements stay fixed in number as n grows, giving constant auxiliary storage for A, B and D. Buffered mergesort instead needs a linear auxiliary buffer.

Ordinary array merging needs a linear auxiliary buffer.DSA37

D · correct — One saved item and fixed-size indices suffice while larger entries shift within the original array.

Correct answers (select all): A, D — A. Bubble sort; D. Merge sort

Strict bubble swaps never exchange equal adjacent keys, so equal records retain their input order. Left-first handling during merging likewise preserves the order of ties from the left and right runs. Standard selection sort can reverse ties through a distant minimum exchange, and ordinary quicksort partitioning does not guarantee stable order. The specified implementation details therefore make bubble and merge the two stable choices.

stack usually log n average, n worst; unstableDSA31

B · incorrect — A distant minimum exchange can reverse equal records.

C · incorrect — Ordinary in-place partitioning does not guarantee stability.

D · correct — Taking the left run first on ties preserves equal-key order.

Correct answer: D — D. Radix sort

Strings can be compared lexicographically, but the stated question asks for a digit-based mechanism rather than whole-key comparisons. Study-guide references

Correct answer: B — N-1

The first element is already a sorted prefix. Each of the remaining N-1 elements is inserted once: the source starts with the first two, then adds the third, and so on. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 3.

Begin with the first element already sorted. For each remaining item, save its value, shift larger preceding values right, and insert it into the gap. That gives n-1 insertion passes. Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA33 · Selection sort: minimize exchanges, not comparisons

Correct answer: C — C. Large values need to be sorted with small keys

Selection sort scans suffixes and makes quadratic comparisons regardless of the initial order, but it performs at most one meaningful exchange per placement. That tradeoff can be useful when physically moving a large record is expensive while comparing its small key is cheap. A large file or sorted input alone does not offer this advantage. Expensive large-key comparisons instead make selection’s many comparisons less attractive.

Evidence in the complete study note

At position i, scan the remaining suffix for its minimum, then exchange it with A[i]. There are n-1 meaningful placements and n(n-1)/2 comparisons regardless of initial order. At most n-1 exchanges of distinct positions are needed. A loop that also swaps the last item with itself can count n swap calls.DSA33

Choice by choice

B · incorrect — Large file size alone does not identify the expensive-move advantage.

D · incorrect — Expensive comparisons with cheap moves do not favor that tradeoff.

Study-guide references

DSA37 · Merge sort and internal versus external sorting

Correct answer: A — Sorting using external storage such as disk or tape.

DSA37 defines external sorting through datasets beyond main memory and buffered disk runs. Option A captures this distinguishing external-storage use. Main memory may still hold buffers, but using it alone does not define external sorting. Swapping and being in place are separate implementation properties and do not identify whether the working dataset resides externally.

Evidence in the complete study note

Top-down mergesort recurses; bottom-up merges runs of widths 1,2,4,… iteratively. In-place merging variants exist with different tradeoffs; linear merge names an operation, not a universally standardized sort variant. Internal sorting fits the working dataset in memory. External sorting builds sorted runs and merges buffered streams from disk, aiming to reduce I/O. Reverse order alone does not characterize maximum merge comparisons.DSA37

DSA32 identifies quadratic average and worst work from repeated adjacent comparisons. Under the usual random-permutation average model, bubble sort therefore takes Θ(n²), which implies O(n²). Fix the input size before comparing cases. Best-case cost is the minimum resource use over legal inputs of that size; worst-case cost is the maximum. These three input-case functions can each be described using upper, lower or tight asymptotic bounds; the case name does not select the bound notation.DSA-S01

DSA06 · Upper, lower and tight bounds

Correct answer: A — A. O(n log n)

Ordinary mergesort splits the array into logarithmically many levels and performs linear total merging work per level. It therefore has n log n worst-case growth under the specified implementation. Sorted input does not skip any merges here. The quadratic and n² log n choices are looser upper bounds, while n(log n)² grows faster than n log n. For eventually nonnegative functions, f(n)=O(g(n)) means f(n)≤c g(n) for some positive c beyond a threshold k. Omega reverses the inequality; Theta requires both. Little-o means f/g tends to zero; little-omega means it grows without bound. These relations can describe best-case, average-case, worst-case or space functions.DSA06

DSA06 · Upper, lower and tight bounds

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA37 · Merge sort and internal versus external sorting

DSA06 · Upper, lower and tight bounds

Correct answer: A — A. O(n log n)

Ordinary mergesort splits the array into logarithmically many levels and performs linear total merging work per level. It therefore has n log n best-case growth under the specified implementation. Sorted input does not skip any merges here. The quadratic and n² log n choices are looser upper bounds, while n(log n)² grows faster than n log n. Asking for the tightest listed bound selects A uniquely.

Evidence in the complete study note

There are logarithmically many levels with linear merge work per level, giving n log n time even on sorted input unless an optimization skips merges.DSA37
For eventually nonnegative functions, f(n)=O(g(n)) means f(n)≤c g(n) for some positive c beyond a threshold k. Omega reverses the inequality; Theta requires both. Little-o means f/g tends to zero; little-omega means it grows without bound. These relations can describe best-case, average-case, worst-case or space functions.DSA06

Choice by choice

A · correct — This matches the actual n log n growth.

B · incorrect — Quadratic is a valid but looser upper bound.

C · incorrect — n² log n is a valid but looser upper bound.

D · incorrect — n(log n)² grows faster and is a looser upper bound.

Using the terminology of the course note, which listed phrase names the combining operation rather than a recognized organization or storage variant of mergesort?

Study-guide sections

DSA37 · Merge sort and internal versus external sorting

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA37 · Merge sort and internal versus external sorting

Correct answer: D — D. linear merge sort

Top-down mergesort recursively divides the sequence, while bottom-up mergesort iteratively combines runs of increasing widths. In-place variants change the storage tradeoff used while merging. Under the note’s stated terminology, linear merge names the combining operation itself rather than a separate standardized sort variant. This is a distinction within the supplied naming convention, not a claim that no author could ever use that phrase differently.

Evidence in the complete study note

Top-down mergesort recurses; bottom-up merges runs of widths 1,2,4,… iteratively. In-place merging variants exist with different tradeoffs; linear merge names an operation, not a universally standardized sort variant. Internal sorting fits the working dataset in memory. External sorting builds sorted runs and merges buffered streams from disk, aiming to reduce I/O. Reverse order alone does not characterize maximum merge comparisons.DSA37

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — In-place merging is a recognized storage variant.

B · incorrect — Bottom-up mergesort is the iterative run-merging organization.

C · incorrect — Top-down mergesort is the recursive organization.

D · correct — Linear merge names the combining operation under the stated terminology.

Study-guide references

DSA32 · Bubble sort: complete adjacent passes

DSA37 · Merge sort and internal versus external sorting

DSA31 · Compare sorting rules, not just algorithm names

Correct answer: A — Standard quicksort is unstable.

The DSA31 sorting table identifies quicksort as unstable. Cocktail and bubble sorts preserve equal-key order when swapping only strict adjacent inversions. Ordinary merge sort preserves equal-key order when ties are taken from the left run first. Under these usual implementations, quicksort is the single listed algorithm that does not guarantee stability.

Evidence in the complete study note

Early stopping makes a sorted input linear: one no-swap pass finishes. A fixed pass schedule stays quadratic. Strict swaps preserve equal-key order. Cocktail sort runs bubble passes in both directions and is stable with strict swaps.DSA32
With left-first tie handling, equal keys retain order.DSA37
stack usually log n average, n worst; unstableDSA31

D · incorrect — Merge sort preserves equal-key order by taking equal elements from the left run first.

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA36 · Quicksort: separate partition guarantees from exact traces

Correct answer: C — C. median-of-three partitioning

On a strictly increasing array, the first key is the minimum and the last key is the maximum, so those deterministic endpoint rules choose extremes. The median of the first, middle and last keys is the middle-position value, which is neither extreme for the stated size. A random element is not a deterministic rule and can choose an endpoint. This criterion selects C without claiming a universally best practical pivot strategy.

Evidence in the complete study note

Choose a pivot, partition, then recursively sort the pieces. Balanced partitions give n log n work; repeated extreme pivots sum n+(n-1)+… to quadratic work. Expected n log n needs an input/random-pivot model. Random and median-of-three choices have different tradeoffs; neither is universally best.DSA36

Correct answer: D — Both short lists and a single unsorted-list query favor scanning.

Linear scanning can suit a short list because setup costs may dominate, and it can answer a single unsorted query without first building an ordered index or sorting the data. Question 60

What is the worst case complexity of binary search using recursion?

  • A. O(nlogn)
  • B. O(logn)
  • C. O(n)
  • D. O(n2)

Source

  • Data Structures & Algorithms practice questions · Question 40

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Study-guide sections

DSA29 · Binary search: maintain a shrinking ordered interval

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA29 · Binary search: maintain a shrinking ordered interval

Correct answer: B — O(logn)

Each recursive step halves the candidate interval; after k steps its size is at most n/2^k. Reaching size one requires about log2 n steps. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 3.

Evidence in the complete study note

On an ascending random-access sequence, set lo=0, hi=n-1. Compute mid=lo+(hi-lo)//2. Equality finishes; if target<A[mid], set hi=mid-1; otherwise set lo=mid+1. Stop unsuccessfully when lo>hi. Reverse comparisons for descending order. Comparable keys and valid finite bounds matter; fixed allocation before population is not an extra algorithmic requirement.DSA29
Worst probes are floor(log₂n)+1 for n>0: seven for 100 keys, about twenty for one million. Iteration uses constant space; recursion uses logarithmic stack depth. Linked midpoint traversal loses logarithmic total time. Boundary variants retain a candidate rather than stopping at equality.DSA29

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — n log n overcounts a single search path. See assigned PDF 3.

B · correct — Repeated halving gives logarithmic search depth. See assigned PDF 3.

C · incorrect — Linear ignores the discarded half at every step. See assigned PDF 3.

D · incorrect — Quadratic has no corresponding nested scan. See assigned PDF 3.

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA29 · Binary search: maintain a shrinking ordered interval

Correct answer: D — D. Directly searching an unordered list without sorting or an ordered index

Binary search needs ordering that justifies rejecting one half of its candidate interval. Lower and upper bounds in an ordered sequence have that property. Searching sorted interval endpoints during an interval-union task also supplies an ordered subproblem, and a monotone debugging boundary permits the same halving logic. Direct searching in an unordered list supplies no such invariant, so a midpoint comparison cannot safely discard a half.

On an ascending random-access sequence, set lo=0, hi=n-1. Compute mid=lo+(hi-lo)//2. Equality finishes; if target<A[mid], set hi=mid-1; otherwise set lo=mid+1. Stop unsuccessfully when lo>hi. Reverse comparisons for descending order. Comparable keys and valid finite bounds matter; fixed allocation before population is not an extra algorithmic requirement.DSA29

DSA02 · Arrays: indexed access, capacity and shifting

DSA18 · Tree vocabulary and the different binary shapes

Correct answer: A — A. linked list

The payload stores an item and the successor link connects its node to the next item’s node. Following those links produces a linear sequence ending at null, which is the ordinary singly linked-list representation. An array instead reaches equal-sized positions by address arithmetic, and a binary tree has a branching parent/child contract rather than this one-successor sequence contract. The linked-list option is therefore the matching standard name.

A singly linked node contains data and next. Head points to the first node; null ends a noncircular chain.DSA08
For equal-size elements, address(A[i]) = base + i × element_size under zero-based indexing.DSA02
Binary means at most two children.DSA18

Study-guide references

DSA08 · Understand the linked-node chain

DSA02 · Arrays: indexed access, capacity and shifting

Correct answer: D — D. Array implementation with a separate logical-position-to-node index

Ordinary singly, doubly and circular linked lists must follow links to reach a logical position, giving linear worst-case positional access. Storing nodes in an array alone does not change that. The explicit extra index in D is different: it maps each logical position directly to the corresponding node, so a random-access array lookup answers the query in constant time. Update costs are excluded by the stated workload.

To display or count nodes, follow next from head until null, processing each node. Counting is Theta(n) unless size is maintained. An array-linked list still follows links unless separately position-indexed.DSA08
For equal-size elements, address(A[i]) = base + i × element_size under zero-based indexing. This arithmetic gives constant-time positional access in the usual RAM cost model. A row-major rectangular matrix uses base + (row × columns + column) × element_size.DSA02

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Ordinary next-link traversal is linear in the worst case.

B · incorrect — Using either endpoint still requires linear worst-case traversal.

C · incorrect — Circular links do not supply a direct logical-position index.

D · correct — The maintained position-to-node array permits direct indexed lookup.

A serial-storage interface restricts insertion and removal to the same current end: an item must be removed before any item stored earlier beneath it can be removed. Which ADT matches this restricted access policy?

DSA45 · State trace data and representation assumptions

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA11 · Implement a stack with one consistent top convention

DSA45 · State trace data and representation assumptions

Correct answer: D — D. Stack

The restriction makes the latest inserted item the next removable item. That is the stack’s LIFO policy, with both push and pop acting at the top. Serial access alone would not establish this rule, so the same-end removal restriction is stated explicitly. A heap selects by priority, a binary tree supplies branching relationships, and an ordinary array permits indexed access rather than imposing this removal policy.

Evidence in the complete study note

Stack policy is LIFO, equivalently FILO. Push inserts, pop removes/returns top, and peek only observes. With zero-based occupied slots, top=-1 is empty and top=C-1 is full. Check before A[++top]=x or returning A[top--].DSA11
ADTs do not force one representation, and serial-access memory is not inherently LIFO.DSA45

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — A heap selects an extreme priority rather than the latest insertion.

Question 75

A singly linked queue maintains only its front pointer and owns all its nodes. Emptying means immediately visiting and freeing every node. Which option gives the complete set of listed operations with tight worst-case linear time for n nodes?

  • A. Insertion
  • B. Deletion
  • C. To empty a queue
  • D. Both Insertion and To empty a queue

Adapted from

  • Data Structures & Algorithms practice questions · Question 55

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Fix the input case and cost model, then count dominant work or simultaneously live storage.

Study-guide sections

DSA14 · Queues preserve arrival order

DSA09 · Update links without losing the rest of the list

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA14 · Queues preserve arrival order

DSA09 · Update links without losing the rest of the list

Correct answer: D — D. Both Insertion and To empty a queue

Enqueue must traverse from the front to find the tail because no rear pointer is maintained. Emptying the owned queue must also visit and release all n nodes under the specified reclamation contract. Deleting one front node requires only a constant number of link and deallocation operations. Therefore both insertion and complete emptying are linear, and the aggregate option D is the complete selection.

Evidence in the complete study note

An ordinary queue enqueues at rear, dequeues at front, and peeks at front. This is FIFO or first-come, first-served. A linked implementation with head and tail supports both operations in constant time: append at tail, remove at head. The first insertion sets both pointers; removing the last item clears both. With head alone, insertion must traverse to the tail.DSA14
Deleting the tail of a singly linked list requires its predecessor, even when tail itself is known. Handle empty and single-node lists separately; after removing the only node, set both head and tail to null. To remove a known successor, bypass it before deallocation. Clearing an owned n-node chain visits and releases every node.DSA09

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Insertion is linear, but this omits the also-linear emptying operation.

B · incorrect — A single front deletion is constant time.

C · incorrect — Emptying is linear, but this omits insertion.

D · correct — Both insertion and immediate full-node cleanup are linear.

DSA41 · BFS: discover one distance layer at a time

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA41 · BFS: discover one distance layer at a time

Correct answer: B — Queue

DSA41 repeatedly dequeues a vertex and enqueues undiscovered neighbors. FIFO service preserves the order of distance layers. Queue is therefore the standard BFS frontier structure. A linked list may store the queue but does not alone define this ordering; a stack chooses latest pending work and instead supports the depth-first discipline.

Evidence in the complete study note

Mark the source when enqueuing it. Repeatedly dequeue a vertex, examine its neighbours, and enqueue each unvisited neighbour while marking it. Store predecessor[v] when discovering v if a path must be reconstructed. FIFO ensures vertices at distance d are explored before later distance layers.DSA41

C · incorrect — Linked nodes can store a queue, but linked-list structure alone specifies no BFS frontier policy.

D · incorrect — Queue is offered and directly matches the algorithm given in DSA41.

Correct answers (select all): A, B — A. Allow duplicate keys; B. Cannot be traversed

A map associates each unique key with a value. Different keys may share the same value, and its entries can be traversed even when a particular iteration order is not promised. DSA18 · Tree vocabulary and the different binary shapes

DSA19 · BST search follows a global ordering invariant

Correct answers (select all): A, C — A. Every node has at most two children.; C. Every node stores a unique key value.

Binary limits a node to at most two children; it does not require every node to have exactly two. The specified distinct-key model also requires uniqueness. A and C consequently hold under the stated model, while B and the all-of-the-above aggregate do not.

Evidence in the complete study note

Binary means at most two children. Full means each node has zero or two children. Complete means all earlier levels are filled and the last fills from left. Perfect means all leaves share a level and every internal node has two children. Balanced means height stays logarithmic under a stated rule; it does not require a perfect shape.DSA18
With distinct keys, every key in a node’s left subtree is smaller and every key in its right subtree is larger. Immediate-child comparisons alone are insufficient: root 10, left child 5, and 5’s right child 12 violate the root’s restriction. Duplicates require a separate count or placement policy.DSA19

Choice by choice

A · correct — Binary means at most two children per node.

B · incorrect — An equal key violates the specified strict left-subtree ordering.

C · correct — Distinct keys mean every stored key value is unique.

D · incorrect — B is false, so not all preceding statements hold.

During ordinary lookup in a binary search tree with distinct keys and strict left-smaller/right-larger ordering, which rule correctly chooses the next subtree or recognizes a match?

DSA19 · BST search follows a global ordering invariant

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA19 · BST search follows a global ordering invariant

Correct answer: A — A. If the searched key is less than the root, go to left.

The BST invariant puts every key in the current node’s left subtree below that node’s key and every right-subtree key above it. A target smaller than the current key must therefore be sought on the left. A larger target belongs on the right, while equality finishes the lookup at the current node. This directional rule relies on BST ordering, not merely on having a binary shape.

Evidence in the complete study note

With distinct keys, every key in a node’s left subtree is smaller and every key in its right subtree is larger. Immediate-child comparisons alone are insufficient: root 10, left child 5, and 5’s right child 12 violate the root’s restriction. Duplicates require a separate count or placement policy.DSA19

Choice by choice

A · correct — A smaller target follows the left subtree under the BST invariant.

B · incorrect — A larger target follows right, not left.

C · incorrect — Equality is a successful match rather than a reason to continue left.

D · incorrect — A supplies a valid search rule.

Infix notation places each binary operator between its two operands, using precedence rules and parentheses to establish grouping. Question 103

Which task requires FIFO service rather than the LIFO service of a stack used as the sole pending-item ADT? In D, asynchronous transfer must deliver buffered items in arrival order.

  • A. String reversal
  • B. Recursion
  • C. Backtracking
  • D. Asynchronous buffered transfer with mandatory arrival-order delivery

Adapted from

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Compare the required operations, access order and representation metadata with each option.

Study-guide sections

DSA12 · Trace stack operations and reversible actions

DSA14 · Queues preserve arrival order

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA12 · Trace stack operations and reversible actions

DSA14 · Queues preserve arrival order

Correct answer: D — D. Asynchronous buffered transfer with mandatory arrival-order delivery

Stacks support reversal by popping items in reverse insertion order. They also manage nested recursive calls and backtracking through the most recent pending context or choice. The stated asynchronous-transfer contract instead requires older buffered items to be delivered before newer arrivals. That is FIFO service, so an ordinary queue supplies the needed ordering. A single stack’s LIFO removal rule does not meet this explicitly ordered buffering contract.

Evidence in the complete study note

Calls nest on a runtime stack; the latest call returns first. Bracket matching pushes opening brackets and matches each closing bracket against top. Reversal pushes input then pops it. Undo moves the latest action from undo to redo; redo moves it back. A new edit after undo normally clears redo. DFS and backtracking use the same latest-pending-choice discipline.DSA12
FIFO suits equal-priority printer jobs, shared-resource waiting, asynchronous buffers and level-order exploration. A play sequence can also use a queue. Distinguish airline seat records from waiting requests; an application name alone does not force one representation.DSA14

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Reversal uses the stack’s reverse insertion order.

B · incorrect — Nested recursive calls return most-recent-first.

C · incorrect — Backtracking resumes the latest pending choice.

D · correct — Arrival-order delivery requires FIFO rather than a single stack’s LIFO.

Question 104

For an unordered symbol table with no range queries, assume suitable hashing and bounded load factor. Which listed ordinary representation offers expected constant-time lookup, compared with linear list search and logarithmic balanced-tree search?

  • A. Self-organizing list
  • B. Hash table
  • C. Balanced search tree
  • D. Linear list scan

Adapted from

  • Computer Science model exam 2 · Question 49

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Compare the required operations, access order and representation metadata with each option.

Study-guide sections

DSA27 · Maps, sets and caches specify different contracts

DSA26 · Resolve collisions and watch the load factor

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA27 · Maps, sets and caches specify different contracts

DSA26 · Resolve collisions and watch the load factor

Correct answer: B — B. Hash table

Symbol tables can use hashing for expected constant lookup when hashing spreads keys suitably and load remains bounded. Balanced search trees supply logarithmic lookup and ordering, while list search can require a linear scan. The comparison concerns the expected lookup growth under those assumptions, not an unconditional worst-case minimum. Collision-heavy hash inputs can still take linear time outside that expected analysis.

Evidence in the complete study note

A dictionary or compiler symbol table can use hashing for expected constant lookup, or a balanced tree for logarithmic lookup with ordering. A bounded cache also needs eviction rules: FIFO uses a queue; LRU can combine hash lookup with a doubly linked recency list. Move a hit to the recent end and evict the least-recent end when full. No storage structure is universally best without operation and policy requirements.DSA27
Separate chaining stores colliding entries in a bucket list. Load alpha=n/m is average chain length; expected operations are O(1+alpha) under suitable distribution assumptions, with O(n) worst cases. Open addressing keeps entries inside the array and probes until a key or an available slot is found.DSA26

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Ordinary self-organizing list search does not guarantee the stated general expected bound.

B · correct — Suitable hashing with bounded load provides expected constant lookup.

C · incorrect — A balanced search tree has logarithmic lookup.

D · incorrect — A linear list scan takes linear worst-case lookup.

Study-guide references

DSA40 · Graphs: represent the relationships you actually need

Correct answer: D — Directed Acyclic Graph

DSA40 directly expands DAG to directed acyclic graph. Directed specifies that each edge has an orientation, and acyclic excludes directed cycles. Detecting, Data, and Dynamic do not supply the defined first word. This is a vocabulary question and does not depend on graph representation or a particular traversal algorithm.

A graph has vertices V and edges E. Directed edges distinguish u→v from v→u; undirected edges represent two-way relationships. Following accounts is directed; a mutual friendship relation is undirected. Weighted edges carry costs; unweighted shortest-path questions count edges. DAG expands to directed acyclic graph. Trees are connected acyclic graphs, although graph data structures may also contain cycles.DSA40

Question 108

A binary search tree was built by inserting the following numbers in the given order: 40, 20, 50, 10, 30, 60. Which of the following statements are true?

  • A. 30 is the left child of 40
  • B. the tree is a heap
  • C. height of the tree is 3
  • D. 50 is the right child of 40

Source

  • Mock exam 1 · Question 13

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Compare the required operations, access order and representation metadata with each option.

Study-guide sections

DSA19 · BST search follows a global ordering invariant

DSA18 · Tree vocabulary and the different binary shapes

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA19 · BST search follows a global ordering invariant

DSA18 · Tree vocabulary and the different binary shapes

Correct answer: D — 50 is the right child of 40

Insertions give root 40; its children 20 and 50; 20 has children 10 and 30; 50 has right child 60. The deepest depth is two edges. A max heap is impossible because child 50 exceeds root 40. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 9, 11.

Evidence in the complete study note

With distinct keys, every key in a node’s left subtree is smaller and every key in its right subtree is larger. Immediate-child comparisons alone are insufficient: root 10, left child 5, and 5’s right child 12 violate the root’s restriction. Duplicates require a separate count or placement policy.DSA19
A rooted tree has one parentless root and one parent per other node. It is connected and acyclic, has n-1 edges, and one path between any pair. Depth counts root-to-node edges; height is maximum depth. A single-node tree therefore has height zero. Leaves have no children.DSA18

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — 30 is the right child of 20, not the left child of 40. See assigned PDF 9, 9, 9, 11.

B · incorrect — 50 exceeds its parent 40, violating the module max-heap rule. See assigned PDF 9, 9, 9, 11.

C · incorrect — Height is depth two, not the three-level count. See assigned PDF 9, 9, 9, 11.

D · correct — 50 is larger than 40 and becomes its right child. See assigned PDF 9, 9, 9, 11.

An owning dynamically allocated linked-list API must provide item search, insertion and removal. Removal unlinks and frees its node before returning; it returns any needed payload by value. Which additional function is unnecessary and would violate the contract if its result were dereferenced?

  • A. A function that returns a pointer to an already freed node for later dereferencing
  • B. A function that searches for an item from the list

Study-guide sections

DSA03 · Operations, records and memory ownership

DSA09 · Update links without losing the rest of the list

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA03 · Operations, records and memory ownership

DSA09 · Update links without losing the rest of the list

Correct answer: A — A. A function that returns a pointer to an already freed node for later dereferencing

The API explicitly requires search, insertion and removal, so those operations belong in its interface. Its removal contract frees the node before returning, leaving that node’s storage unavailable for later dereference. An additional function promising a usable pointer to the freed node is therefore inappropriate. Returning a copied payload is different and remains allowed; the distinction concerns storage lifetime rather than whether deletion may report a value.

Evidence in the complete study note

A C struct groups named fields, including arrays and pointers. A singly linked node needs payload plus a same-type link. C fields cannot have initializers inside the type declaration; modern C++ permits default member initializers. In C++, match new with delete and new[] with delete[]. Repair links before freeing a node; never dereference it afterwards.DSA03
Prepend with new.next=head; head=new. To insert after a known predecessor p, set new.next=p.next before p.next=new. Appending with only head requires a tail traversal; maintaining tail avoids it. Delete the head by saving old=head, advancing head=head.next and releasing old in C++.DSA09

Choice by choice

A · correct — A usable pointer to a freed node violates the stated lifetime contract.

B · incorrect — Item search is explicitly required by this API.

C · incorrect — Item insertion is explicitly required by this API.

D · incorrect — Item removal is explicitly required by this API.

E · incorrect — A identifies an inappropriate extra function.

Question 112

Consider a max-heap of n>=3 distinct keys, stored in ordinary level-order array form. Its binary tree is full: every internal node has two children. Which statement is false?

  • A. The root is the biggest element.
  • B. The second biggest element is necessarily found at depth 1 (root is at depth 0)
  • C. The search for the smallest element can be accomplished in O(log n) time (worst case)
  • D. The last element of the array is necessarily the right most child on the lowest level.

Adapted from

  • Mock exam 3 · Question 11

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Compare the required operations, access order and representation metadata with each option.

Study-guide sections

DSA23 · A heap combines completeness with a weaker ordering

DSA18 · Tree vocabulary and the different binary shapes

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA23 · A heap combines completeness with a weaker ordering

DSA18 · Tree vocabulary and the different binary shapes

Correct answer: C — C is false: finding the minimum can require Theta(n) time.

The root contains the maximum key. With distinct keys, the second largest must be one of its children, since a deeper key has a larger ancestor above it. Completeness places the final occupied array slot at the rightmost occupied position of the lowest level. The minimum can occur at any leaf, however, so finding it may require a linear scan rather than logarithmic worst-case time. C is therefore false.

Evidence in the complete study note

A binary max-heap is complete with each parent at least its children; a min-heap reverses this order. Unlike BSTs, heaps do not order entire subtrees. The root is maximum. If all keys are distinct, the second largest is a root child. With duplicate maxima, the second largest distinct value may be deeper: [9,9,9,8,7,6,5] is a valid max-heap and that value is 8 at index 3. The minimum may be any leaf, requiring linear worst-case scanning.DSA23
Complete means all earlier levels are filled and the last fills from left.DSA18

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — The max-heap order makes the root the largest key, so this is true rather than the requested false statement.

B · incorrect — Distinct keys ensure the second largest is a root child, so this is true.

C · correct — The minimum may require scanning linearly many leaves; the logarithmic worst-case claim is false.

D · incorrect — Level-order storage of a complete heap ends at the rightmost occupied position on the lowest level.

  • B. When the list is already sorted in the "right" order

Study-guide sections

DSA37 · Merge sort and internal versus external sorting

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA37 · Merge sort and internal versus external sorting

Correct answer: E — E. None of the choices is correct

Maximum merge comparisons depend on the interleaving of the sorted runs, rather than merely on a broad input label. Sorted or reverse-sorted input produces separated runs, and equal keys let left-first merging exhaust a run early. Distinct keys permit a worst interleaving but do not force one; already sorted distinct keys are a counterexample. None of A–D therefore guarantees the requested exact maximum.

Evidence in the complete study note

Split into halves, sort them, then merge by advancing the smaller current front. With left-first tie handling, equal keys retain order. Ordinary array merging needs a linear auxiliary buffer. There are logarithmically many levels with linear merge work per level, giving n log n time even on sorted input unless an optimization skips merges.DSA37
Reverse order alone does not characterize maximum merge comparisons.DSA37

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Reverse order alone does not force worst interleavings.

B · incorrect — Sorted runs can be merged with an early exhaustion of one side.

C · incorrect — Left-first equal keys exhaust a run without maximum interleaving.

D · incorrect — Distinct keys can already be sorted, so distinctness is insufficient.

E · correct — No preceding description alone guarantees the exact maximum comparison count.

Correct answer: E — E. Array

An array computes an element address from its base address, the requested index and the fixed element size, giving constant-time access. Answer & Detailed Explanation

DSA19 · BST search follows a global ordering invariant

DSA29 · Binary search: maintain a shrinking ordered interval

DSA23 · A heap combines completeness with a weaker ordering

Correct answers (select all): A, E — A. Height-balanced BST; E. Sorted random-access array with binary search

A height-balanced BST has logarithmic height, so following its ordered search path takes logarithmic worst-case time. A sorted random-access array supports logarithmic binary-search probes. An ordinary singly linked list must traverse links, and a heap does not order entire subtrees by arbitrary search keys. Thus the combined A-and-C claim fails because C lacks the guarantee, while A and E independently meet it.

Evidence in the complete study note

Search compares at each node and follows one child until equality or null. Insertion uses that same path to attach a new leaf. Operations cost O(height): logarithmic for balanced trees, linear for a chain. Best-case successful search is Theta(1), a root hit. An optimal BST minimizes expected search cost using access probabilities; constructing it is a different problem from searching it.DSA19
Worst probes are floor(log₂n)+1 for n>0: seven for 100 keys, about twenty for one million. Iteration uses constant space; recursion uses logarithmic stack depth. Linked midpoint traversal loses logarithmic total time. Boundary variants retain a candidate rather than stopping at equality.DSA29
Unlike BSTs, heaps do not order entire subtrees.DSA23

E · correct — Binary search on a sorted random-access array is logarithmic.

DSA37 · Merge sort and internal versus external sorting

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA37 · Merge sort and internal versus external sorting

Correct answer: B — Sorting whose working dataset fits in main memory.

DSA37 defines internal sorting by fitting the working dataset in memory. Option B expresses that main-memory setting. In contrast, external sorting handles disk-backed runs when data exceeds memory. Swapping is an operation used by some algorithms, and in-place describes auxiliary storage; neither determines whether a sort is internal.

Evidence in the complete study note

Top-down mergesort recurses; bottom-up merges runs of widths 1,2,4,… iteratively. In-place merging variants exist with different tradeoffs; linear merge names an operation, not a universally standardized sort variant. Internal sorting fits the working dataset in memory. External sorting builds sorted runs and merges buffered streams from disk, aiming to reduce I/O. Reverse order alone does not characterize maximum merge comparisons.DSA37

DSA36 · Quicksort: separate partition guarantees from exact traces

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA36 · Quicksort: separate partition guarantees from exact traces

Correct answer: B — B. O(n^2)

An extreme pivot leaves one empty part and one part with only a single element removed. Repeating that pattern makes partition work proportional to n+(n-1)+… rather than distributing it across balanced levels. The sum is quadratic. Balanced partitions explain the n log n alternative, but they are not guaranteed in this worst case. Exponential time is a looser upper bound, not the tightest listed one.

Evidence in the complete study note

Choose a pivot, partition, then recursively sort the pieces. Balanced partitions give n log n work; repeated extreme pivots sum n+(n-1)+… to quadratic work. Expected n log n needs an input/random-pivot model. Random and median-of-three choices have different tradeoffs; neither is universally best.DSA36

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Linear time does not cover repeated partition scans.

B · correct — Repeated extreme pivots produce quadratic total work.

C · incorrect — Exponential is a much looser upper bound.

D · incorrect — n log n requires suitably balanced or expected partitions.

  • A. In universal hashing a hash function is selected randomly from a set of hash functions for each key
  • B. In universal hashing a hash function is selected from a set of hash functions independent of keys
  • C. A single fixed hash function is always better than universal hashing at reducing collisions.
  • D. Universal hashing controls collision probability without guaranteeing zero collisions.
