Study-guide sections

DSA25 · Hash addresses, uniformity and random function choice

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA25 · Hash addresses, uniformity and random function choice

Correct answers (select all): A, C — A. In universal hashing a hash function is selected randomly from a set of hash functions for each key; C. A single fixed hash function is always better than universal hashing at reducing collisions.

Universal hashing chooses one random function for the table and then uses it consistently, rather than selecting an unrelated function afresh for each key. Its purpose is to control collision probability for a fixed key set. It does not establish that a single fixed function is always better for avoiding collisions. Thus A and C are false, while independent table-level choice and probability control are the valid principles.

Evidence in the complete study note

Determinism means repeated equal keys get the same address for the chosen function. Uniformity means expected keys spread evenly. Universal hashing chooses one function randomly from a suitable family for the table, independently of a fixed key set; it does not choose a fresh unrelated function for each lookup. Random choice controls collision probability, not a promise of zero collisions.DSA25

Choice by choice

A · correct — The chosen function is reused for the table rather than chosen afresh per key.

B · incorrect — Independence from the fixed key set is the stated selection principle.

C · correct — Unconditional fixed-function superiority does not follow and contradicts the randomized collision-control purpose.

D · incorrect — Universal choice controls collision probability without promising no collisions.

DSA42 · DFS: finish a branch before returning

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA42 · DFS: finish a branch before returning

Correct answer: D — Stack

DSA42 says DFS recursively explores an unvisited neighbor to completion before returning. The recursive call stack stores return points; an explicit stack can store pending work instead. Both implement latest-pending-work-first order. A queue would change that discipline, while a priority queue or tree alone does not encode the required depth-first frontier behavior.

Evidence in the complete study note

Mark a vertex, then recursively visit each unmarked neighbour before continuing with later neighbours. An explicit stack can store pending work instead. Both implement latest-pending-work first; a queue would change that discipline. Marking prevents infinite repetition around graph cycles.DSA42

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Priority service follows priority keys and does not guarantee finishing the latest active branch first.

B · incorrect — A tree may represent traversal results, but it does not identify the standard DFS pending-work discipline.

C · incorrect — FIFO queue order produces breadth-first pending work rather than the required latest-pending-work behavior.

D · correct — A stack, explicit or supplied by recursion, preserves return points and latest-pending-work-first order.

A singly linked list of n nodes maintains only its head; there is no tail pointer or index. Appending traverses to the last node before linking a new node. Which listed bounds hold for its worst-case time? Select all that apply.

  • A. O(n)
  • B. Theta(1)
  • C. Theta(n)
  • D. O(1)

Study-guide sections

DSA09 · Update links without losing the rest of the list

DSA06 · Upper, lower and tight bounds

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA09 · Update links without losing the rest of the list

DSA06 · Upper, lower and tight bounds

Correct answers (select all): A, C — A. O(n); C. Theta(n)

The append operation begins at the head and must follow the chain to locate its final node. That requires linear traversal, followed by a constant amount of link work. Its tight worst-case bound is therefore Theta(n), which also implies the upper bound O(n). Neither constant-time choice holds as the list grows. Maintaining a separate tail would change the operation cost, but that representation is explicitly excluded.

Evidence in the complete study note

Prepend with new.next=head; head=new. To insert after a known predecessor p, set new.next=p.next before p.next=new. Appending with only head requires a tail traversal; maintaining tail avoids it. Delete the head by saving old=head, advancing head=head.next and releasing old in C++.DSA09
For eventually nonnegative functions, f(n)=O(g(n)) means f(n)≤c g(n) for some positive c beyond a threshold k. Omega reverses the inequality; Theta requires both. Little-o means f/g tends to zero; little-omega means it grows without bound. These relations can describe best-case, average-case, worst-case or space functions.DSA06

Choice by choice

A · correct — O(n) is a valid upper bound on the traversal.

B · incorrect — The growing traversal prevents a constant tight bound.

C · correct — Theta(n) is the tight traversal bound.

D · incorrect — O(1) does not bound arbitrary head-only append traversal.

DSA29 · Binary search: maintain a shrinking ordered interval

DSA28 · Linear search: a scan with an early stop

DSA25 · Hash addresses, uniformity and random function choice

DSA42 · DFS: finish a branch before returning

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA29 · Binary search: maintain a shrinking ordered interval

DSA28 · Linear search: a scan with an early stop

DSA25 · Hash addresses, uniformity and random function choice

DSA42 · DFS: finish a branch before returning

Correct answer: C — C. Binary search

Binary search compares a target with the midpoint of an ordered interval, then safely discards one half. That elimination depends on sorted order. Linear search can scan unsorted values, hashing selects addresses from keys rather than sorted positions, and depth-first search follows graph adjacency. The revised alternatives therefore have clear operational meanings, and Binary search uniquely matches the stated ordered-half-elimination requirement.

Evidence in the complete study note

On an ascending random-access sequence, set lo=0, hi=n-1. Compute mid=lo+(hi-lo)//2. Equality finishes; if target<A[mid], set hi=mid-1; otherwise set lo=mid+1.DSA29
Unsorted data is allowed; sorted data is allowed too.DSA28
A hash table uses h(key) in 0..m-1 and stores only actual entries plus bucket capacity.DSA25
Mark a vertex, then recursively visit each unmarked neighbour before continuing with later neighbours.DSA42

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Hash lookup uses computed addresses rather than a sorted input interval.

B · incorrect — Depth-first search follows adjacency, not ordered-array halves.

C · correct — Binary search needs ordering to safely discard a comparison-selected half.

D · incorrect — Linear scanning permits unsorted input.

Study-guide references

DSA19 · BST search follows a global ordering invariant

DSA20 · Tree traversal is a rule you can execute

Correct answer: C — In-order

All left-subtree keys precede the root, and all right-subtree keys follow it. Recursively visiting left, parent, right therefore emits increasing keys. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 9.

Evidence in the complete study note

With distinct keys, every key in a node’s left subtree is smaller and every key in its right subtree is larger. Immediate-child comparisons alone are insufficient: root 10, left child 5, and 5’s right child 12 violate the root’s restriction. Duplicates require a separate count or placement policy.DSA19
Preorder visits node,left,right; inorder left,node,right; postorder left,right,node. Apply recursively; null children do nothing. Inorder returns sorted keys only for a BST. Preorder supports copying, postorder supports deleting children before parents, and level order uses a FIFO queue.DSA20

D · incorrect — Postorder prints the root after larger right keys. See assigned PDF 9, 9.

Study-guide sections

DSA15 · Circular buffers: logical order differs from physical slots

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA15 · Circular buffers: logical order differs from physical slots

Correct answer: C — C. O(1), O(1)

Enqueue computes a slot from front and size, writes one item and updates the count. Dequeue reads the front slot, advances front modulo capacity and decreases the count. Full or empty checks also inspect only constant-size state. No operation shifts or resizes the array, so each uses constant work in the stated model. The linear alternatives are looser bounds rather than the requested tight pair.

Evidence in the complete study note

A simple noncircular array queue may report overflow when rear reaches the final index despite released slots at the front. A circular queue reuses slots with modulo arithmetic. Use a count convention: front points to the next removal, size counts items, and insertion slot is (front+size)%C. Empty means size==0; full means size==C.DSA15
Dequeue reads A[front], sets front=(front+1)%C and decreases size. An alternative reserves one unused slot and uses next(rear)==front for full; its empty test and capacity differ. State the convention before tracing.DSA15

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Linear enqueue is looser than the constant cost of this implementation.

B · incorrect — Linear dequeue is looser than its constant index update cost.

C · correct — Both endpoint operations use constant work.

D · incorrect — Both linear bounds are looser than the requested tight pair.

A tree is expressly an abstract model of a hierarchical structure, and a binary tree is its at-most-two-children specialization. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 9.

A rooted tree has one parentless root and one parent per other node. It is connected and acyclic, has n-1 edges, and one path between any pair. Depth counts root-to-node edges; height is maximum depth. A single-node tree therefore has height zero. Leaves have no children.DSA18

DSA12 · Trace stack operations and reversible actions

Correct answer: A — Stack

Backtracking is explicitly listed as a stack application: the latest pending decision can be undone first using pop. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 7, 6.

Evidence in the complete study note

Calls nest on a runtime stack; the latest call returns first. Bracket matching pushes opening brackets and matches each closing bracket against top. Reversal pushes input then pops it. With head alone, insertion must traverse to the tail.DSA14

DSA41 · BFS: discover one distance layer at a time

Correct answer: B — Queue

DSA41 enqueues discovered neighbors and dequeues the next pending vertex. This FIFO discipline preserves distance-layer ordering. A linked list can store the queue but does not by itself state the policy. Stack service is latest-first, while a binary tree is not the standard frontier discipline. Evidence in the complete study note

Mark the source when enqueuing it. Repeatedly dequeue a vertex, examine its neighbours, and enqueue each unvisited neighbour while marking it. Calls nest on a runtime stack; the latest call returns first. Bracket matching pushes opening brackets and matches each closing bracket against top. Reversal pushes input then pops it. Undo moves the latest action from undo to redo; redo moves it back. A new edit after undo normally clears redo. DFS and backtracking use the same latest-pending-choice discipline.DSA12

A · correct — Push records actions; pop undoes the most recent; a second LIFO stack supports redo. See assigned PDF 7, 6.

B · incorrect — FIFO would undo the oldest pending action first. See assigned PDF 7, 6.

D · incorrect — A binary tree does not directly supply last-action-first reversal. See assigned PDF 7, 6.

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA12 · Trace stack operations and reversible actions

DSA11 · Implement a stack with one consistent top convention

Correct answer: A — A. Stack

A stack accepts the sequence in arrival order and then removes the most recently inserted item first. Repeated pops therefore emit the complete reverse sequence directly. A FIFO queue preserves the original order. A generic linked list or binary tree does not itself specify the required removal discipline; reversing existing links would be a separate algorithm excluded by this question. The contract identifies the auxiliary reversal ADT.

Evidence in the complete study note

Calls nest on a runtime stack; the latest call returns first. Bracket matching pushes opening brackets and matches each closing bracket against top. Reversal pushes input then pops it. Undo moves the latest action from undo to redo; redo moves it back. A new edit after undo normally clears redo. DFS and backtracking use the same latest-pending-choice discipline.DSA12
Stack policy is LIFO, equivalently FILO. Push inserts, pop removes/returns top, and peek only observes. With zero-based occupied slots, top=-1 is empty and top=C-1 is full. Check before A[++top]=x or returning A[top--].DSA11

Choice by choice

A · correct — Push all items and then pop to emit reverse order directly.

DFS finishes the most recently entered unfinished branch before returning to older pending work. A stack directly supplies this latest-pending-work-first rule. Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA17 · Priority queues serve by priority, with an explicit tie rule

Correct answers (select all): C, D — C. Linked list; D. Binary tree organized as a binary heap

A priority queue removes an item with an extreme priority key. An unordered list can scan for that extremum, while an ordered list maintains the relevant order during insertion. A binary heap supplies the same priority contract through heap order and logarithmic insertion/extraction. An unmodified stack or FIFO queue removes according to arrival position rather than priority. Thus the list and heap-shaped binary tree qualify under the stated algorithms.

Evidence in the complete study note

A priority queue returns the smallest or largest priority key under its convention. Urgent patients may precede earlier arrivals. Insertions and extractions can interleave. Binary heaps support constant peek and logarithmic insert/extract.DSA17
Arrays and lists can also implement priority queues: an unordered sequence gives cheap insertion but linear extremum removal; an ordered sequence reverses that tradeoff. Equal priorities have no inherent FIFO guarantee. If stable service is required, compare (priority, arrival_counter). Choose the priority direction and tie rule before tracing.DSA17

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — An unmodified stack removes by recency rather than priority.

B · incorrect — An unmodified FIFO queue removes by arrival order rather than priority.

C · correct — Ordered or scanned lists can select the extreme priority.

D · correct — A binary heap implements priority selection through heap order.

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA14 · Queues preserve arrival order

DSA11 · Implement a stack with one consistent top convention

Correct answer: B — B. Queue

The ordinary queue inserts new items at its rear and removes or observes the front item. These restrictions produce FIFO service: earlier arrivals are removed before later arrivals. A stack uses a single top and LIFO order. A general linked list permits operations beyond these restricted endpoints, while a binary tree organizes hierarchical relationships. Specifying the exact operations resolves the original vague use of access.

Evidence in the complete study note

An ordinary queue enqueues at rear, dequeues at front, and peeks at front. This is FIFO or first-come, first-served. A linked implementation with head and tail supports both operations in constant time: append at tail, remove at head. The first insertion sets both pointers; removing the last item clears both. With head alone, insertion must traverse to the tail.DSA14
Stack policy is LIFO, equivalently FILO. Push inserts, pop removes/returns top, and peek only observes. With zero-based occupied slots, top=-1 is empty and top=C-1 is full. Check before A[++top]=x or returning A[top--].DSA11

DSA19 · BST search follows a global ordering invariant

DSA22 · Balanced trees prevent the sorted-input chain

DSA-S03 · Linked nodes and multiway tree branching

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA19 · BST search follows a global ordering invariant

DSA22 · Balanced trees prevent the sorted-input chain

DSA-S03 · Linked nodes and multiway tree branching

Correct answer: B — B. Binary search tree

The global left-smaller/right-larger invariant defines the binary search tree family. It applies to every descendant in each subtree, not only immediate children. AVL and red-black trees satisfy that ordering but impose additional balancing disciplines, so they are more specialized than the family requested. The binary-tree restriction also excludes a general B-tree. Asking for the most general family prevents those BST subclasses from becoming competing selections.

Evidence in the complete study note

With distinct keys, every key in a node’s left subtree is smaller and every key in its right subtree is larger. Immediate-child comparisons alone are insufficient: root 10, left child 5, and 5’s right child 12 violate the root’s restriction. Duplicates require a separate count or placement policy.DSA19
AVL balance factor is height(left)-height(right); every node must have factor -1,0 or 1. After insertion or deletion, update heights upward and rotate where necessary. LL imbalance needs a right rotation; RR needs left; LR rotates the left child left then the node right; RL is symmetric. Rotations preserve inorder key order.DSA22
A B-tree is a balanced multiway search tree. Its allowed branching factor can exceed two, so a general B-tree is not the binary-tree family. Balanced describes a height discipline; it does not by itself restrict every node to two children.DSA-S03

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — AVL adds balance requirements beyond the stated invariant.

B · correct — BST is the general family defined by the strict subtree ordering alone.

C · incorrect — Red-black trees add a balancing discipline beyond the stated invariant.

D · incorrect — A general B-tree is not the requested binary-tree family.

Question 170

A bounded FIFO buffer must reuse freed array slots by wrapping indices modulo its fixed capacity, without shifting items. New insertions are rejected while full. Which listed term specifically names this storage representation?

  • A. Stack
  • B. Queue
  • C. Linked list
  • D. Circular buffer

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA15 · Circular buffers: logical order differs from physical slots

DSA16 · Deques, merging and splitting queues

Correct answer: D — D. Circular buffer

A circular buffer reuses its fixed slots by wrapping indices modulo capacity, so released positions can be used again without moving surviving items. The FIFO order is tracked logically rather than by requiring the front to remain at physical slot zero. Queue names the service ADT and can have other representations; it does not specifically identify this layout. Stack and linked list likewise do not name the stated circular-array representation.

Evidence in the complete study note

A simple noncircular array queue may report overflow when rear reaches the final index despite released slots at the front. A circular queue reuses slots with modulo arithmetic. Use a count convention: front points to the next removal, size counts items, and insertion slot is (front+size)%C. Empty means size==0; full means size==C.DSA15
Merging FIFO queues needs an explicit policy: append one sequence after another or alternate their fronts. Splitting by a predicate preserves each subgroup’s original order if each removed item is appended to its matching output queue. A fixed-capacity buffer also needs a full-policy choice: reject, block or overwrite. Capacity alone does not choose a policy.DSA16

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — A stack names LIFO service rather than the specified FIFO ring storage.

B · incorrect — Queue names the FIFO ADT but does not specifically identify its storage layout.

C · incorrect — A linked list does not name modulo-indexed circular array slots.

D · correct — Circular buffer specifically names the stated fixed-slot wraparound representation.

DSA37 · Merge sort and internal versus external sorting

DSA34 · Insertion sort: extend a sorted prefix

Correct answer: C — C. Merge sort

Mergesort divides the array into two halves, recursively sorts them and merges their results, so it uses divide and conquer. Ordinary bubble sort uses adjacent passes and selection sort repeatedly selects a suffix minimum. The explicitly specified LSD radix method performs stable digit passes rather than recursive subproblem decomposition. This convention removes the possible confusion with MSD radix grouping while retaining the original primary answer.

Evidence in the complete study note

Divide and conquer reduces a problem to smaller instances of the same kind, solves the required smaller instances and obtains the original result from them. Mergesort recursively sorts two halves and merges; quicksort partitions and recursively sorts the resulting ranges. This course also classifies binary search as divide and conquer: an ordered comparison selects the only half that can contain the target. This is different from simply repeating adjacent swaps, choosing successive minima, or making stable LSD digit passes.DSA-S04
LSD radix sorting handles fixed-width digit keys by stably sorting least-significant digit first, then moving left. Stable intermediate passes preserve the ordering already established by less-significant digits. With d digits and radix r, counting-based passes take O(d(n+r)) time and O(n+r) auxiliary storage.DSA39
Begin with the first element already sorted. For each remaining item, save its value, shift larger preceding values right, and insert it into the gap.DSA34

Quicksort partitions around a pivot and recursively sorts the smaller ranges. Top-down mergesort recursively sorts halves and merges their results. Both therefore apply divide and conquer. Bubble sort’s adjacent passes and ordinary insertion sort’s growing sorted prefix do not use this recursive subproblem decomposition. The complete answer is B and C; the question requires multiple selection.

Correct answers (select all): C, D — C. Radix sort; D. Merge sort

Stable LSD radix passes preserve the ordering already established by less significant digits. Equal full keys remain tied on every pass, so their relative order remains unchanged. Question 175

Which searching algorithm is based on comparing the target value with elements at midpoints of the array?

  • A. Linear search
  • B. Binary search
  • C. Interpolation search
  • D. Depth-first search

Source

  • Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 439

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Compare the algorithmic steps and access policy with the exact resource or ordering requirement in the question.

Study-guide sections

DSA29 · Binary search: maintain a shrinking ordered interval

DSA30 · Search variants need their own assumptions

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA29 · Binary search: maintain a shrinking ordered interval

DSA30 · Search variants need their own assumptions

Correct answer: B — Binary search

DSA29 computes the midpoint of the current ordered interval, compares it with the target, and discards the half that cannot contain the target. That is exactly the midpoint-based procedure in the stem. Linear search scans successive elements, interpolation estimates a position from values, and DFS follows graph branches rather than ordered-array midpoints.

Evidence in the complete study note

On an ascending random-access sequence, set lo=0, hi=n-1. Compute mid=lo+(hi-lo)//2. Equality finishes; if target<A[mid], set hi=mid-1; otherwise set lo=mid+1. Stop unsuccessfully when lo>hi. Reverse comparisons for descending order. Comparable keys and valid finite bounds matter; fixed allocation before population is not an extra algorithmic requirement.DSA29
Interpolation search estimates the index from numeric values: lo+(hi-lo)×(key-A[lo])/(A[hi]-A[lo]), rounded to a valid index. Guard equal endpoints and out-of-range targets. On sorted, suitably uniform data its expected probes can be O(log log n); pathological distributions can require linear time. Binary search gives a logarithmic worst bound without that distribution assumption.DSA30

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Linear search compares successive elements rather than repeatedly choosing the midpoint of a shrinking ordered interval.

B · correct — Binary search explicitly compares the target with the current interval midpoint and keeps one half.

C · incorrect — Interpolation search estimates a probe from numeric values and their distribution, rather than always using the midpoint.

D · incorrect — Depth-first search explores graph neighbors and branches, not ordered-array midpoint intervals.

Correct answers (select all): C, D — C. Depth-first search; D. Breadth-first search

DFS explores an unvisited branch before returning to later neighbors, using recursion or a stack. BFS instead processes a FIFO frontier so successive distance layers are explored in order. Linear sequence scanning and binary interval search are different algorithms and do not implement these two adjacency-frontier traversal disciplines.

Mark the source when enqueuing it. Repeatedly dequeue a vertex, examine its neighbours, and enqueue each unvisited neighbour while marking it. Store predecessor[v] when discovering v if a path must be reconstructed. FIFO ensures vertices at distance d are explored before later distance layers.DSA41
Mark a vertex, then recursively visit each unmarked neighbour before continuing with later neighbours. An explicit stack can store pending work instead. Both implement latest-pending-work first; a queue would change that discipline. Marking prevents infinite repetition around graph cycles.DSA42

DSA25 · Hash addresses, uniformity and random function choice

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA29 · Binary search: maintain a shrinking ordered interval

DSA25 · Hash addresses, uniformity and random function choice

Correct answer: B — Binary search

DSA29 defines binary search over an ascending random-access sequence and reverses comparisons for descending data. Sortedness makes the half-elimination step sound. Linear scanning works without order; hashing needs a built table rather than sorted positions; DFS follows adjacency. Only Binary search among this option set requires a sorted input sequence for its ordinary operation.

Evidence in the complete study note

On an ascending random-access sequence, set lo=0, hi=n-1. Compute mid=lo+(hi-lo)//2. Equality finishes; if target<A[mid], set hi=mid-1; otherwise set lo=mid+1. Stop unsuccessfully when lo>hi. Reverse comparisons for descending order. Comparable keys and valid finite bounds matter; fixed allocation before population is not an extra algorithmic requirement.DSA29
Direct addressing reserves a position for every possible key in a finite universe U, costing Theta(|U|) slots. A hash table uses h(key) in 0..m-1 and stores only actual entries plus bucket capacity. With h(k)=k mod 6, key 36 has home address 0; collisions may move its final storage position.DSA25

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Linear search explicitly permits unsorted data and compares items one after another.

B · correct — Binary search relies on ordered values to determine which half can still contain the target.

C · incorrect — Hash lookup needs a hash-table organization, not values arranged in sorted-array order.

D · incorrect — Depth-first search follows graph or tree adjacency and does not require a sorted input array.

Study-guide sections

DSA29 · Binary search: maintain a shrinking ordered interval

DSA28 · Linear search: a scan with an early stop

DSA26 · Resolve collisions and watch the load factor

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA29 · Binary search: maintain a shrinking ordered interval

DSA28 · Linear search: a scan with an early stop

DSA26 · Resolve collisions and watch the load factor

Correct answer: B — Binary search has logarithmic worst-case time.

DSA29 bounds binary-search probes by floor(log₂n)+1 on nonempty random-access input. This supplies logarithmic worst-case time under constant-cost comparisons. Linear search may scan all items; adverse hash collisions may require linear work; DFS can inspect all vertices and edges. Their ordinary worst cases do not share binary search’s logarithmic bound.

Evidence in the complete study note

Worst probes are floor(log₂n)+1 for n>0: seven for 100 keys, about twenty for one million. Iteration uses constant space; recursion uses logarithmic stack depth. Linked midpoint traversal loses logarithmic total time. Boundary variants retain a candidate rather than stopping at equality.DSA29
Compare the target with successive elements until equal or exhausted. Unsorted data is allowed; sorted data is allowed too. A first-element match costs Theta(1). An absent target or last-position match needs n comparisons, giving Theta(n) worst time. Uniformly likely successful positions average (n+1)/2 comparisons, still linear.DSA28
Separate chaining stores colliding entries in a bucket list. Load alpha=n/m is average chain length; expected operations are O(1+alpha) under suitable distribution assumptions, with O(n) worst cases. Open addressing keeps entries inside the array and probes until a key or an available slot is found.DSA26

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Linear search can inspect every item when the target is absent or last, giving linear worst-case time.

B · correct — Each comparison discards about half the ordered interval, giving logarithmic worst-case probes.

C · incorrect — Ordinary hash lookup can degrade to linear time under adverse collisions, despite expected constant-time performance.

D · incorrect — DFS may visit all graph vertices and edges, rather than guarantee logarithmic worst-case work.

DSA42 · DFS: finish a branch before returning

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA42 · DFS: finish a branch before returning

Correct answer: D — Depth-first search

DSA42 describes marking a vertex and recursively visiting each unmarked neighbor before resuming later neighbors. That procedure is standard depth-first traversal and applies to graphs and trees. Linear search scans a sequence, binary search uses an ordered interval, and hash search queries table addresses. None of those alternatives names the adjacency-following traversal in this option set.

Evidence in the complete study note

Mark a vertex, then recursively visit each unmarked neighbour before continuing with later neighbours. An explicit stack can store pending work instead. Both implement latest-pending-work first; a queue would change that discipline. Marking prevents infinite repetition around graph cycles.DSA42

B · incorrect — Binary search reduces an ordered interval rather than visiting arbitrary graph or tree connections.

C · incorrect — Hash search probes key-derived table addresses rather than traversing graph or tree edges.

D · correct — DFS follows unvisited neighbors recursively or through an explicit stack, providing a standard traversal.

Correct answers (select all): A, C, D — A. Bubble sort; C. Merge sort; D. Insertion sort

Bubble sort’s strict adjacent swaps do not exchange equal keys. Mergesort preserves ties by taking an equal key from the left run first. Insertion sort shifts only strictly larger keys, leaving equal earlier keys ahead of the inserted one. Those three mechanisms preserve relative equal-key order. Ordinary in-place quicksort does not guarantee it because partition exchanges can move equal records past one another.

Correct answer: B — Binary search

DSA29 compares the middle value with the target and continues only in the half that can contain it. This solves a smaller instance of the same ordered-search problem and is the divide-and-conquer reduction intended here. Linear scanning removes one candidate at a time, hashing computes addresses, and DFS follows adjacency without this ordered half-elimination rule.

Evidence in the complete study note

Divide and conquer reduces a problem to smaller instances of the same kind, solves the required smaller instances and obtains the original result from them. Mergesort recursively sorts two halves and merges; quicksort partitions and recursively sorts the resulting ranges. This course also classifies binary search as divide and conquer: an ordered comparison selects the only half that can contain the target. This is different from simply repeating adjacent swaps, choosing successive minima, or making stable LSD digit passes.DSA-S04
On an ascending random-access sequence, set lo=0, hi=n-1. Compute mid=lo+(hi-lo)//2. Equality finishes; if target<A[mid], set hi=mid-1; otherwise set lo=mid+1. Stop unsuccessfully when lo>hi. Reverse comparisons for descending order. Comparable keys and valid finite bounds matter; fixed allocation before population is not an extra algorithmic requirement.DSA29

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA37 · Merge sort and internal versus external sorting

Correct answer: C — Merge sort using buffered external runs.

DSA37 describes external sorting by building sorted runs and merging buffered disk streams to reduce I/O. Merge sort naturally supports that strategy even when the whole dataset does not fit RAM. Bubble and insertion sorting repeatedly move local data, while ordinary quicksort assumes partition access rather than the external sequential-run pattern specified here.

Evidence in the complete study note

Top-down mergesort recurses; bottom-up merges runs of widths 1,2,4,… iteratively. In-place merging variants exist with different tradeoffs; linear merge names an operation, not a universally standardized sort variant. Internal sorting fits the working dataset in memory. External sorting builds sorted runs and merges buffered streams from disk, aiming to reduce I/O. Reverse order alone does not characterize maximum merge comparisons.DSA37

Study-guide references

Correct answer: C — C. Hash search

Hash lookup computes a bucket or probe start from the key and uses the existing index to locate an equality match. With suitable distribution and bounded load, the note gives expected constant lookup. The important assumptions are the index and workload, rather than dataset size alone. Linear scanning ignores the index, binary search needs an ordered interval, and DFS follows graph relationships instead of this equality-key access structure.

Evidence in the complete study note

Separate chaining stores colliding entries in a bucket list. Load alpha=n/m is average chain length; expected operations are O(1+alpha) under suitable distribution assumptions, with O(n) worst cases. Open addressing keeps entries inside the array and probes until a key or an available slot is found.DSA26
A dictionary or compiler symbol table can use hashing for expected constant lookup, or a balanced tree for logarithmic lookup with ordering. A bounded cache also needs eviction rules: FIFO uses a queue; LRU can combine hash lookup with a doubly linked recency list. Move a hit to the recent end and evict the least-recent end when full. No storage structure is universally best without operation and policy requirements.DSA27

Study-guide references

DSA43 · Shortest paths and spanning trees solve different objectives

DSA41 · BFS: discover one distance layer at a time

Correct answer: C — C. Dijkstra's algorithm

Standard Dijkstra repeatedly finalizes the unsettled vertex with the smallest tentative distance and relaxes its outgoing edges. Nonnegative edge weights justify this shortest-path procedure even when different edges have different costs. BFS minimizes edge count and is sufficient when edge costs are equal, which is weaker than the stated guarantee. DFS supplies reachability paths, while Prim minimizes total spanning-tree cost rather than source-to-vertex route lengths.

Evidence in the complete study note

For nonnegative weights, standard Dijkstra initializes source distance zero and others infinity, repeatedly finalizes the unsettled vertex with smallest distance, and relaxes each outgoing edge: dist[v]=min(dist[v],dist[u]+w(u,v)). A min-priority queue supports the next choice. BFS is enough when every edge has equal cost; negative edges require another justified method, such as Bellman–Ford.DSA43
BFS finds minimum-edge paths in unweighted graphs, not arbitrary minimum-weight paths.DSA41

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — A DFS path need not have minimum total weight.

B · incorrect — BFS minimizes edge count and does not guarantee minimum weight for arbitrary differing costs.

C · correct — Dijkstra guarantees source shortest paths under nonnegative weights.

D · incorrect — Prim solves the spanning-tree objective rather than source shortest paths.

The array representation maintains a top index and changes it when pushing or popping. Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA27 · Maps, sets and caches specify different contracts

DSA10 · Doubly linked, circular and practical list choices

Correct answer: B — B. Doubly linked list with head and tail

The hash index handles locating an entry, while the recency component must unlink a known entry and reconnect it at the recent end. A doubly linked list supplies both neighboring links for that constant-time removal and maintains endpoints for movement and eviction. An array would generally shift entries, a bare hash table does not supply recency order, and an ordinary FIFO queue cannot remove an arbitrary known interior entry.

Evidence in the complete study note

A dictionary or compiler symbol table can use hashing for expected constant lookup, or a balanced tree for logarithmic lookup with ordering. A bounded cache also needs eviction rules: FIFO uses a queue; LRU can combine hash lookup with a doubly linked recency list. Move a hit to the recent end and evict the least-recent end when full. No storage structure is universally best without operation and policy requirements.DSA27
Doubly linked nodes add prev; head and tail enable constant-time operations at both ends. Singly linked tail deletion still needs its predecessor. A circular tail links back to head; stop traversal on returning to the start, handling empty separately.DSA10

B · correct — A doubly linked recency list supports unlinking a known node and endpoint updates.

Question 202

Which algorithm is used to find the maximum subarray sum in an array?

  • B. Quick sort

DSA44 · Recognize two other tested algorithms through their rules

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA44 · Recognize two other tested algorithms through their rules

Correct answer: D — Kadane’s algorithm

DSA44 directly identifies Kadane as the contiguous maximum-sum-subarray algorithm. It updates the best sum ending at the current item and the best sum seen overall, using linear time and constant working storage. Binary search does not optimize contiguous sums, and quicksort or merge sort reorder values rather than preserve the original adjacency needed by this problem.

Evidence in the complete study note

Kadane’s algorithm finds a contiguous maximum-sum subarray. For a required nonempty answer, initialize ending=best=A[0]; update ending=max(x,ending+x), then best=max(best,ending). It is linear time with constant working storage. Initializing best=0 instead silently allows an empty answer and fails the nonempty all-negative case.DSA44

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Binary search locates targets or ordered boundaries; it does not compute a contiguous maximum-sum subarray.

B · incorrect — Quicksort reorders values and does not preserve the original adjacency required for maximum subarray sum.

C · incorrect — Merge sort orders values; the named sorting algorithm is not the maximum-subarray recurrence.

D · correct — Kadane maintains the best sum ending here and the best anywhere, directly solving the stated problem.

DSA43 · Shortest paths and spanning trees solve different objectives

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA43 · Shortest paths and spanning trees solve different objectives

Correct answer: D — Prim’s algorithm

DSA43 defines an MST as a minimum-total-cost connection of all vertices in a connected undirected weighted graph. Prim repeatedly adds the cheapest edge crossing from its current tree to an outside vertex. Dijkstra minimizes source-path distances instead, while BFS and DFS are traversals without a general minimum-weight spanning-tree guarantee. Thus Prim is the listed MST algorithm.

Evidence in the complete study note

An MST minimizes the total cost of connecting all vertices of a connected undirected weighted graph. Prim adds the cheapest edge crossing from its current tree to an outside vertex. Kruskal processes edges by increasing weight and rejects those joining vertices already connected. An MST need not give shortest source-to-vertex routes, and equal weights can permit several MSTs.DSA43
For nonnegative weights, standard Dijkstra initializes source distance zero and others infinity, repeatedly finalizes the unsettled vertex with smallest distance, and relaxes each outgoing edge: dist[v]=min(dist[v],dist[u]+w(u,v)). A min-priority queue supports the next choice. BFS is enough when every edge has equal cost; negative edges require another justified method, such as Bellman–Ford.DSA43

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — DFS can produce a spanning tree but does not generally minimize total edge weight.

B · incorrect — BFS produces minimum-edge source layers in unweighted graphs, not a general minimum-weight spanning tree.

C · incorrect — Dijkstra minimizes source-to-vertex distances, a different objective from total spanning-tree connection cost.

D · correct — Prim grows a spanning tree by repeatedly choosing a cheapest edge crossing to an outside vertex.

DSA17 · Priority queues serve by priority, with an explicit tie rule

Correct answer: C — C. Binary heap

A binary heap exposes the extreme key at its root, so peek is constant, and insertion or extraction restores order along a logarithmic-height path. Ordinary unordered arrays or lists need a linear search for an extreme, while ordered versions pay linear insertion in the general case. An unmodified FIFO queue follows arrival order rather than priority. The stated operation bounds make the heap the unique matching standard representation.

Arrays and lists can also implement priority queues: an unordered sequence gives cheap insertion but linear extremum removal; an ordered sequence reverses that tradeoff. DSA44 · Recognize two other tested algorithms through their rules

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA44 · Recognize two other tested algorithms through their rules

Correct answer: D — Knuth–Morris–Pratt

DSA44 explicitly defines KMP as finding a pattern inside text. It preprocesses longest proper prefix/suffix lengths and uses them to avoid restarting comparisons after mismatch, giving linear combined pattern-and-text work. DFS, BFS, and Dijkstra concern graph exploration or paths, rather than this specialized substring-matching mechanism. KMP uniquely matches the question among these choices.

Evidence in the complete study note

Knuth–Morris–Pratt (KMP) finds a pattern inside text. Preprocess the pattern’s longest proper prefix that is also a suffix. After mismatch, fall back using those prefix lengths rather than restarting comparisons from the beginning; the text pointer need not move backward. Pattern preprocessing plus scanning takes O(pattern length+text length).DSA44

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — DFS explores graph or tree branches; it is not the substring-pattern algorithm identified in DSA44.

C · incorrect — Dijkstra computes nonnegative weighted shortest paths, not substring pattern occurrences.

D · correct — KMP is the pattern-matching algorithm using preprocessed prefix/suffix lengths to avoid repeated text comparisons.

Assume a very large finite key universe U but only n stored keys, with n much smaller than |U|. A hash table uses capacity proportional to n. Compare allocated storage, rather than unconditional speed. Which statement is false?

DSA25 · Hash addresses, uniformity and random function choice

Study-guide references

DSA25 · Hash addresses, uniformity and random function choice

Correct answer: C — C. Hash table allocates one separate memory slot for each key in the universe U

Direct addressing reserves a distinct slot for every possible key in the universe, whether present or absent, so its storage is proportional to |U|. The specified hash table stores the actual entries plus capacity proportional to n. For this sparse-universe storage comparison, hashing uses less space. C incorrectly attributes the direct-address allocation rule to hashing, while direct key-to-slot mapping and separate universe slots accurately describe direct addressing.

Evidence in the complete study note

Direct addressing reserves a position for every possible key in a finite universe U, costing Theta(|U|) slots. A hash table uses h(key) in 0..m-1 and stores only actual entries plus bucket capacity. With h(k)=k mod 6, key 36 has home address 0; collisions may move its final storage position.DSA25

Question 210

Which method can resolve collision in hashed files by proceeding from the occupied position specified by the hash address and checking subsequent positions until an empty position is found?

  • A. Open addressing
  • B. Multiple hashing
  • C. Chaining
  • D. Cluster indexing

Source

  • Computer Science Exit Exam practice collection · Question 133

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.

Study-guide sections

DSA26 · Resolve collisions and watch the load factor

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA26 · Resolve collisions and watch the load factor

Correct answer: A — Open addressing, specifically linear probing.

DSA26 defines open addressing as keeping entries within the array and probing until an available slot is found. Checking successive positions is its linear-probing form. Multiple hashing changes probe steps, chaining stores collisions in bucket lists, and cluster indexing is not this insertion procedure. Therefore Open addressing is the matching general method among the options.

Evidence in the complete study note

Separate chaining stores colliding entries in a bucket list. Load alpha=n/m is average chain length; expected operations are O(1+alpha) under suitable distribution assumptions, with O(n) worst cases. Open addressing keeps entries inside the array and probes until a key or an available slot is found.DSA26
Linear probing tries (h(k)+j)%m. For size 7 and keys 10,17,24, all home addresses are 3 and occupied positions become 3,4,5. Quadratic probing changes the step; double hashing uses h1(k)+j h2(k), modulo m, with a step relatively prime to m to cover all slots. Neither method guarantees no collisions. Deletion needs tombstones or reinsertion so searches do not stop prematurely.DSA26

Choice by choice

A · correct — Open addressing searches alternative table positions; checking successive positions is its linear-probing form.

B · incorrect — Multiple or double hashing derives another probe step rather than the stated simple successive-slot scan.

C · incorrect — Chaining puts colliding entries in a bucket list instead of searching successive array slots.

D · incorrect — Cluster indexing does not name the collision insertion strategy described by the successive-position probing rule.

DSA18 · Tree vocabulary and the different binary shapes

Correct answer: D — There is only one unique path when we traverse from one node to another node in a tree

A rooted tree gives every nonroot node exactly one parent and a unique root path. Between any two nodes, ascend to their common ancestor and descend; a second distinct path would create a cycle and violate the parent/path hierarchy. Evidence: assigned PDF pages 9, 2.

A rooted tree has one parentless root and one parent per other node. It is connected and acyclic, has n-1 edges, and one path between any pair. Depth counts root-to-node edges; height is maximum depth. A single-node tree therefore has height zero. Leaves have no children.DSA18

Question 214

Which abbreviations name the stack service policy? Select all that apply.

  • A. LIFO
  • B. FIFO

DSA11 · Implement a stack with one consistent top convention

DSA14 · Queues preserve arrival order

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA11 · Implement a stack with one consistent top convention

DSA14 · Queues preserve arrival order

Correct answers (select all): A, C — A. LIFO; C. FILO

The most recently pushed item is removed first by a stack. This is last in, first out, abbreviated LIFO. Equivalently, the first item inserted remains until later items have been removed, making it first in, last out or FILO. FIFO and FCFS instead preserve arrival order in ordinary queue service. Both A and C therefore name the same stack discipline.

Evidence in the complete study note

Stack policy is LIFO, equivalently FILO. Push inserts, pop removes/returns top, and peek only observes. With zero-based occupied slots, top=-1 is empty and top=C-1 is full. Check before A[++top]=x or returning A[top--].DSA11
An ordinary queue enqueues at rear, dequeues at front, and peeks at front. This is FIFO or first-come, first-served. A linked implementation with head and tail supports both operations in constant time: append at tail, remove at head. The first insertion sets both pointers; removing the last item clears both. With head alone, insertion must traverse to the tail.DSA14

Choice by choice

A · correct — LIFO means last in, first out.

B · incorrect — FIFO means first in, first out, an ordinary queue policy.

C · correct — FILO is the equivalent first in, last out view of a stack.

D · incorrect — FCFS describes arrival-order service rather than stack service.

Binary search repeatedly removes roughly half of the remaining candidate interval. The note bounds its worst probes by floor(log₂n)+1 for nonempty input, giving logarithmic worst-case time under constant-cost indexing. The linear, quadratic and n-times-squared-log options all grow faster and are looser upper bounds. Explicitly asking for the tightest bound selects the logarithmic alternative rather than treating every valid Big-O upper bound as equally responsive.

Evidence in the complete study note

Worst probes are floor(log₂n)+1 for n>0: seven for 100 keys, about twenty for one million. Iteration uses constant space; recursion uses logarithmic stack depth. Linked midpoint traversal loses logarithmic total time. Boundary variants retain a candidate rather than stopping at equality.DSA29
For eventually nonnegative functions, f(n)=O(g(n)) means f(n)≤c g(n) for some positive c beyond a threshold k. Omega reverses the inequality; Theta requires both. Little-o means f/g tends to zero; little-omega means it grows without bound. These relations can describe best-case, average-case, worst-case or space functions.DSA06

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — n(log n)² is a much looser upper bound.

B · incorrect — Quadratic is a looser upper bound.

C · incorrect — Linear is a looser upper bound.

D · correct — Logarithmic matches the interval-halving probe growth.

Question 216

Which sorting algorithm compares each pair of adjacent elements from the beginning of an array and, if they are in reversed order, swaps them; if at least one swaps has been done, repeat step 1.

  • A. Insertion sort
  • B. Bubble sort
  • C. Selection sort
  • D. Shell sort

Source

  • Computer Science Exit Exam · 2018 · Question 87

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.

Study-guide sections

DSA32 · Bubble sort: complete adjacent passes

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA32 · Bubble sort: complete adjacent passes

Correct answer: B — Bubble sort with early stopping

DSA32 describes adjacent comparisons, swapping strict inversions, and repeating passes until a pass performs no swaps. That matches every part of the stem, including its stopping condition. Insertion grows a sorted prefix, selection chooses a suffix minimum, and Shell uses separated gap subsequences, so none has this exact adjacent full-pass mechanism.

Evidence in the complete study note

For ascending order, compare each adjacent pair and swap only when left>right. The largest remaining value moves to the final unsorted position after one left-to-right pass. Shrink the next pass by one position. Quadratic worst/average work comes from up to n(n-1)/2 pair comparisons.DSA32

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Insertion places each next value into a sorted prefix rather than repeating full adjacent passes.

B · correct — Adjacent inversion swaps and repetition until no swaps identify optimized bubble sort.

C · incorrect — Selection finds a suffix minimum and exchanges it with the prefix boundary.

D · incorrect — Shell sorts gap-separated subsequences before its final gap-one insertion pass.

Question 217

Among the following one is NOT the application of queue in the real world.

  • A. It is used in operating systems for handling interrupts.
  • B. It is used to maintain the play list in media players in order
  • C. It is used in Depth First search
  • D. It is widely used as waiting lists for a single shared resource

Source

  • Computer Science Exit Exam · 2018 · Question 91

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.

Study-guide sections

DSA42 · DFS: finish a branch before returning

DSA14 · Queues preserve arrival order

DSA-S02 · Queues for deferred interrupt work

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA42 · DFS: finish a branch before returning

DSA14 · Queues preserve arrival order

DSA-S02 · Queues for deferred interrupt work

Correct answer: C — Depth-first search uses stack discipline rather than the ordinary queue.

DSA42 finishes a branch using a stack or recursion and explicitly says a queue changes that discipline. DSA14 gives FIFO waiting, play sequences, and asynchronous buffering as queue uses. Interrupt work can also be buffered pending service. Thus the standard DFS claim is the non-queue application among the offered ordinary examples.

Evidence in the complete study note

Mark a vertex, then recursively visit each unmarked neighbour before continuing with later neighbours. An explicit stack can store pending work instead. Both implement latest-pending-work first; a queue would change that discipline. Marking prevents infinite repetition around graph cycles.DSA42
FIFO suits equal-priority printer jobs, shared-resource waiting, asynchronous buffers and level-order exploration. A play sequence can also use a queue. Distinguish airline seat records from waiting requests; an application name alone does not force one representation.DSA14
An interrupt service routine may need to record work quickly and defer its completion. Operating systems can queue that deferred work for later processing; Windows deferred procedure calls are one concrete example. This is a queue application, but it does not imply that every interrupt system uses a single FIFO service policy.DSA-S02

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Pending interrupts can be buffered for later service; queue use need not imply one universal interrupt priority policy.

B · incorrect — A FIFO play queue can preserve the order of media items.

C · correct — Standard DFS uses latest-pending-work-first stack or recursion rather than FIFO queue service.

D · incorrect — Waiting for one shared resource is a direct FIFO queue application.

DSA01 · Start with the data and the required operations

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

DSA11 · Implement a stack with one consistent top convention

DSA01 · Start with the data and the required operations

Correct answer: C — Stack

DSA11 explicitly assigns LIFO to a stack. Arrays and linked lists can represent that stack, but neither storage structure inherently fixes its removal order. A queue instead supplies FIFO. The question asks for the service-policy ADT, so Stack is the specific answer rather than one of the possible underlying representations.

Evidence in the complete study note

Stack policy is LIFO, equivalently FILO. Push inserts, pop removes/returns top, and peek only observes. With zero-based occupied slots, top=-1 is empty and top=C-1 is full. Check before A[++top]=x or returning A[top--].DSA11
An abstract data type (ADT) defines values and operations; representation supplies implementation. Arrays or linked nodes can implement the same LIFO stack. Abstraction keeps relevant details: patient urgency and arrival order matter for service; hair colour does not.DSA01

A · incorrect — A queue follows FIFO, not the latest-in-first-out order requested.

D · incorrect — A linked list can implement several policies and does not inherently require LIFO.

Question 219

What distinguishes a dynamic data structure from a static one?

    Source

    • Data Structures & Algorithms review questions · Question 2

    Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

    Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.

    Study-guide sections

    DSA02 · Arrays: indexed access, capacity and shifting

    DSA08 · Understand the linked-node chain

    Answer & Detailed Explanation

    Study-guide references

    DSA02 · Arrays: indexed access, capacity and shifting

    DSA08 · Understand the linked-node chain

    Answer: Dynamic structures can change size at runtime; static structures have fixed capacity.

    DSA02 distinguishes fixed arrays from resizable arrays, and DSA08 allocates linked nodes as needed. Runtime growth or shrinkage is the key distinction; fixed capacity need not mean compile-time allocation.

    Evidence in the complete study note

    A fixed array has a chosen capacity; the choice need not occur at compile time. A resizable array allocates a larger block and copies when needed. Inserting in the middle shifts later elements, so it costs linear time. Appending into spare capacity is constant; a resizing append can be linear, though repeated geometric growth gives amortized constant append cost.DSA02
    A singly linked node contains data and next. Head points to the first node; null ends a noncircular chain. Empty means head==null. Nodes allocated as needed grow dynamically, with pointer overhead and no direct index arithmetic.DSA08

          Question 225

          What is the term for the operation that releases memory when a data structure is no longer needed?

            • Data Structures & Algorithms review questions · Question 8

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            DSA03 · Operations, records and memory ownership

            DSA09 · Update links without losing the rest of the list

            Answer: Destruction or deallocation of owned storage.

            DSA03 says destroying a structure releases owned storage. In a linked chain, DSA09 visits and releases each owned node; C++ allocation forms must be matched to their deletion forms, and freed nodes must not be dereferenced.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            A C struct groups named fields, including arrays and pointers. A singly linked node needs payload plus a same-type link. C fields cannot have initializers inside the type declaration; modern C++ permits default member initializers. In C++, match new with delete and new[] with delete[]. Repair links before freeing a node; never dereference it afterwards.DSA03
            Deleting the tail of a singly linked list requires its predecessor, even when tail itself is known. Handle empty and single-node lists separately; after removing the only node, set both head and tail to null. To remove a known successor, bypass it before deallocation. Clearing an owned n-node chain visits and releases every node.DSA09

                  Question 229

                  An algorithm has exactly two independent nested loops. Each executes n iterations, and the innermost body performs constant work. Loop-control operations are constant time, with no early exits or hidden nonconstant operations. What is the tight time complexity as n grows?

                    Adapted from

                    • Data Structures & Algorithms review questions · Question 12

                    Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

                    State the representation and cost model, then count the operations or storage demanded by the question.

                    Study-guide sections

                    DSA07 · Count loops and account for hidden access costs

                    DSA05 · Measure costs before naming their growth

                    Answer & Detailed Explanation

                    Study-guide references

                    DSA07 · Count loops and account for hidden access costs

                    DSA05 · Measure costs before naming their growth

                    Answer: Theta(n²) time.

                    For each of the n outer iterations, the inner loop executes n times, so the constant-cost body runs n×n=n² times. Outer-loop overhead is linear and inner-loop control is also bounded by a constant per body execution. Those contributions do not change the dominant quadratic growth. Under the stated independence, fixed loop count and body-cost assumptions, the tight time complexity is Theta(n²).

                    Evidence in the complete study note

                    A loop i=1; i<n; i*=2 takes about log₂n iterations. Two independent n-iteration loops nested around constant work take Theta(n²). An n-level ordinary recursion with constant live storage per level needs Theta(n) stack space.DSA07
                    Time counts chosen operations; space counts memory, including live recursive frames. Distributed algorithms may also measure communication volume. A single assignment is one unit in the elementary model, not literally one second. Sequential blocks add costs; independent nested loops multiply their iteration counts. Conditional worst-case cost includes the test and the more expensive branch.DSA05

                                Question 237

                                Binary Search requires the list to be:

                                • A. Unsorted
                                • B. Sorted
                                • C. Circular
                                • D. Linked

                                Source

                                • Data Structures & Algorithms review questions · Question 20

                                Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

                                Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.

                                Study-guide sections

                                DSA29 · Binary search: maintain a shrinking ordered interval

                                Answer & Detailed Explanation

                                Study-guide references

                                DSA29 · Binary search: maintain a shrinking ordered interval

                                Correct answer: B — Sorted

                                DSA29 eliminates half an ordered interval according to the midpoint comparison. That elimination is valid only when comparable values follow a consistent order; descending input works with reversed comparisons. Circularity and links are representation properties, not substitutes for sortedness. An unsorted sequence gives no safe smaller-half decision. Therefore Sorted is the required prerequisite.

                                Evidence in the complete study note

                                On an ascending random-access sequence, set lo=0, hi=n-1. Compute mid=lo+(hi-lo)//2. Equality finishes; if target<A[mid], set hi=mid-1; otherwise set lo=mid+1. Stop unsuccessfully when lo>hi. Reverse comparisons for descending order. Comparable keys and valid finite bounds matter; fixed allocation before population is not an extra algorithmic requirement.DSA29

                                Choice by choice

                                A · incorrect — Without order, a midpoint comparison cannot safely eliminate either half.

                                B · correct — Consistent sorted order supports the midpoint half-elimination invariant.

                                C · incorrect — Circular storage does not establish the value ordering needed by binary search.

                                D · incorrect — Linked storage does not imply sortedness and also changes midpoint-access costs.

                                Question 238

                                How many steps does Binary Search take for a list of 1,000,000 elements (approximately)?

                                  Source

                                  • Data Structures & Algorithms review questions · Question 21

                                  Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

                                  Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.

                                  Study-guide sections

                                  DSA29 · Binary search: maintain a shrinking ordered interval

                                  Answer & Detailed Explanation

                                  Study-guide references

                                  DSA29 · Binary search: maintain a shrinking ordered interval

                                  Answer: About 20 worst-case midpoint probes.

                                  DSA29 gives floor(log₂n)+1 probes for n>0. Since 2^19=524288 and 2^20=1048576, one million lies between them, so the worst probe count is twenty under the ordinary interval algorithm. A root/midpoint hit can finish earlier.

                                  Evidence in the complete study note

                                  Worst probes are floor(log₂n)+1 for n>0: seven for 100 keys, about twenty for one million. Iteration uses constant space; recursion uses logarithmic stack depth. Linked midpoint traversal loses logarithmic total time. Boundary variants retain a candidate rather than stopping at equality.DSA29

                                  Question 239

                                  What is the time complexity of Bubble Sort and why?

                                    Source

                                    • Data Structures & Algorithms review questions · Question 22

                                    Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

                                    State the representation and cost model, then count the operations or storage demanded by the question.

                                    Study-guide sections

                                    DSA32 · Bubble sort: complete adjacent passes

                                    Answer & Detailed Explanation

                                    Study-guide references

                                    DSA32 · Bubble sort: complete adjacent passes

                                    Answer: Worst and usual average Θ(n²); early-stop best Θ(n).

                                    DSA32 sums repeated adjacent passes to at most n(n−1)/2 comparisons, yielding quadratic worst and ordinary average work. A no-swap early-stop pass makes sorted input linear, while a fixed pass schedule remains quadratic. The answer needs these implementation and case distinctions.

                                    Evidence in the complete study note

                                    For ascending order, compare each adjacent pair and swap only when left>right. The largest remaining value moves to the final unsorted position after one left-to-right pass. Shrink the next pass by one position. Quadratic worst/average work comes from up to n(n-1)/2 pair comparisons.DSA32

                                    Question 240

                                    In Selection Sort, what does each pass through the unsorted subarray accomplish?

                                      Source

                                      • Data Structures & Algorithms review questions · Question 23

                                      Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

                                      Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.

                                      Study-guide sections

                                      DSA33 · Selection sort: minimize exchanges, not comparisons

                                      Answer & Detailed Explanation

                                      Study-guide references

                                      DSA33 · Selection sort: minimize exchanges, not comparisons

                                      Answer: Select the remaining minimum and put it at the next prefix position.

                                      DSA33 scans the unsorted suffix for its minimum and exchanges it with A[i]. After each meaningful pass, the sorted prefix grows by one and contains the smallest keys placed so far. This differs from inserting the next encountered item into a prefix.

                                      Evidence in the complete study note

                                      At position i, scan the remaining suffix for its minimum, then exchange it with A[i]. There are n-1 meaningful placements and n(n-1)/2 comparisons regardless of initial order. At most n-1 exchanges of distinct positions are needed. A loop that also swaps the last item with itself can count n swap calls.DSA33

                                      Question 241

                                      How does Insertion Sort differ from Selection Sort conceptually?

                                        Source

                                        • Data Structures & Algorithms review questions · Question 24

                                        Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

                                        Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.

                                        Study-guide sections

                                        DSA33 · Selection sort: minimize exchanges, not comparisons

                                        DSA34 · Insertion sort: extend a sorted prefix

                                        Answer & Detailed Explanation

                                        Study-guide references

                                        DSA33 · Selection sort: minimize exchanges, not comparisons

                                        DSA34 · Insertion sort: extend a sorted prefix

                                        Answer: Selection finds a suffix minimum; insertion places the next item into a sorted prefix.

                                        DSA33 chooses the globally smallest remaining key for each next output position. DSA34 instead takes the next input item, shifts larger prefix values, and inserts it into their gap. Both grow sorted prefixes, but choose their next item differently.

                                        Evidence in the complete study note

                                        At position i, scan the remaining suffix for its minimum, then exchange it with A[i]. There are n-1 meaningful placements and n(n-1)/2 comparisons regardless of initial order. At most n-1 exchanges of distinct positions are needed. A loop that also swaps the last item with itself can count n swap calls.DSA33
                                        Begin with the first element already sorted. For each remaining item, save its value, shift larger preceding values right, and insert it into the gap. That gives n-1 insertion passes. On sorted input each pass needs one ordering check and no shifts: linear time. Reverse order causes 1+2+…+(n-1) shifts: quadratic time.DSA34

                                        Question 242

                                        What is the best-case scenario for Bubble Sort and what is its complexity in that case?

                                          Study-guide references

                                          DSA32 · Bubble sort: complete adjacent passes

                                          Answer: Already sorted input; Θ(n) with no-swap early stopping.

                                            Answer: Payload/data and a next-node link.

                                              Question 245

                                              To delete a node from the front of a singly linked list, what single update is needed?

                                                Source

                                                • Data Structures & Algorithms review questions · Question 28

                                                Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

                                                Use the cited definitions and invariants to distinguish the requested concept from related operations.

                                                Study-guide sections

                                                DSA09 · Update links without losing the rest of the list

                                                Answer & Detailed Explanation

                                                Study-guide references

                                                DSA09 · Update links without losing the rest of the list

                                                Answer: Advance head to the old head’s next link, then reclaim the old node.

                                                DSA09 saves old=head, sets head=head.next, and releases old in an owned C++ chain. The essential link update is advancing head; check empty before dereferencing, and clear tail too if the only node was removed. This answers the operation without hiding ownership work.

                                                Evidence in the complete study note

                                                Prepend with new.next=head; head=new. To insert after a known predecessor p, set new.next=p.next before p.next=new. Appending with only head requires a tail traversal; maintaining tail avoids it. Delete the head by saving old=head, advancing head=head.next and releasing old in C++.DSA09
                                                Deleting the tail of a singly linked list requires its predecessor, even when tail itself is known. Handle empty and single-node lists separately; after removing the only node, set both head and tail to null. To remove a known successor, bypass it before deallocation. Clearing an owned n-node chain visits and releases every node.DSA09
